lessons.plain: Before you can watch a system, you have to know what is in it. Analyzing a workload means listing its parts (servers, functions, databases, queues, the network paths between them), noting which parts hold sensitive data or can be reached by outsiders, and deciding what evidence each part should leave behind. Those records are the signals you monitor. If a part that matters leaves nothing behind, you cannot see attacks against it, and that gap is itself a problem to report and fix. This work happens before any tool is switched on, and it decides which tools are worth paying for.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a public web app that reads customer addresses from a database. You can afford to record only three kinds of activity in the first month. Which three would you choose, and why those rather than the busiest parts of the system?
lessons.teach:
A workload is everything that delivers one service: compute (the servers or functions that run code), data stores (databases and object storage), the network paths between them, and the identities that call them. Analyzing a workload means walking through these parts and asking three questions about each: what would an attacker or a fault do here, how bad would that be, and what evidence would show it happening.

Why this works: monitoring costs money, storage, and attention, so recording everything drowns the useful signal. Starting from the parts that matter (those holding sensitive data, those reachable from the internet, and those that grant power over other parts) lets you pick logs and alerts that answer a real question. Different records answer different questions. An audit trail of control-plane changes shows who changed a setting. Network flow records show which addresses talked to which. Application logs show what the code did with a request.

Worked example: a public API sends requests through a load balancer to a function, which reads a customer table. Step 1: list the parts: load balancer, function, table, and the function's execution role. Step 2: the table holds personal data, so data reads and exports matter. Step 3: the role can read the table, so changes to that role's permissions matter. Step 4: the load balancer is public, so unusual request volume matters. Result: change records for the role and table, data access records for the table, and request metrics on the load balancer. A static image bucket with no sensitive content needs only basic access records.

Common mistake: switching on every log type in every account and calling the job done. The volume buries the record that matters, and the bill climbs.

Consequence: if the function's reads from the customer table are not logged, a stolen role could copy the whole table and no alert would fire; the first sign might be a customer complaint. When a part that matters produces no records, report that as a defect and fix it.

The right monitoring list follows from the workload analysis, not from whichever tools happen to be available.

questions.prompt: A team runs a contract-signing service. Customers upload signed PDFs to an upload bucket that only a private endpoint inside the company network can reach. A container service picks each file from a queue, extracts the text, and writes results to a reports bucket. The container's task role can read the upload bucket and write to the reports bucket. Worked so far: Step 1: the parts are the upload bucket, the queue, the container service, the task role, and the reports bucket. Step 2: the upload bucket holds signed contracts, so object read and export records on that bucket matter. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: result: data access records on both buckets, plus change records for the task role.
choices: Step 3: Every log type on the queue should be enabled, because queues carry the files.
Step 3: The private endpoint means the upload bucket needs no monitoring, because nothing outside the network can reach it.
Step 3: The container's CPU and memory usage is the only thing worth recording, because it does all the processing.
Step 3: The task role can read uploads and write reports, so changes to that role's permissions are worth recording.
questions.why: The task role holds power over both buckets, so changes to its permissions are the kind of control-plane record the workload analysis says to keep.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the set of parts that together deliver one service: compute, data stores, the network paths between them, and the identities that call them?
choices: Audit trail
Load balancer
Flow record
Workload
questions.why: A workload is defined in the teaching text as everything that delivers one service, including compute, data stores, network paths, and identities.

questions.prompt: A reporting service has a role that can export a ledger table holding 40,000 customer records. An analyst asks which record would show what the reporting code actually did with a particular request. Which record answers that question?
choices: Control-plane audit trail showing who changed the role's settings
Application logs from the reporting service
Request count metrics on the load balancer in front of it
Network flow records showing which addresses talked to which
questions.why: Application logs show what the code did with a request, while flow records show addresses, audit trails show configuration changes, and metrics show volume only.

questions.prompt: A customer-records database holds sensitive personal data, but its data-access records have produced nothing for three weeks, and no alerts have fired. What is the correct response under the monitoring approach described?
choices: Report the silent database as a defect and restore its records before relying on it
Turn off flow records across the account to lower the monthly bill
Conclude that no alerts means no attack, so no action is needed
Wait for a customer complaint to confirm whether any data was touched
questions.why: When a part that matters produces no records, the teaching text says to report it as a defect and fix it, rather than treating silence as safety.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just turn on every log source in the account so we are covered. Explain to them, in your own words, why analyzing the workload first is better, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd say turning everything on is not coverage, it's noise. First we list the workload's parts: the public entry point, the compute that runs the code, the data stores, the network paths, and the roles that can touch them. For each part we ask what an attacker or a failure would do there and what evidence would show it. Parts holding customer data or reachable from the internet get the richest logs and alerts, while a static asset bucket might only need basic access records. The tradeoff is that this analysis takes time and can miss a part nobody wrote down, so we should check the inventory against the account regularly, and treat any in-scope part that leaves no records as a finding to fix. That keeps cost and alert volume sensible and means every log we keep answers a real question.
rubricPoints: Lists the workload's parts and data flows before choosing which logs to enable.
Ranks parts by sensitivity and exposure, and matches each log type to the question it answers.
Treats a missing log from an in-scope part as a finding to report and fix.
Names a real tradeoff, such as an incomplete inventory or the effort of the analysis itself.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style workload scenario to choose logs and spot gaps adds the most here, since no listed mission covers designing workload monitoring.

lessons.plain: A workload monitoring strategy is a planned set of signals you collect from a running system, such as an app, its servers, or its database, along with how often you check them and what happens when something looks wrong. A resource health check is one kind of signal: an automatic test that asks a component a simple question, like whether it answers correctly, and marks it healthy or unhealthy. Good monitoring combines quick yes-or-no checks with trends over time, so you catch both sudden failures and slow decline before users notice.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app runs on three servers behind a traffic splitter that pings each server every few seconds. Users report errors, but every server still passes its ping. What might the pings be failing to test, and what extra signal would you add?
lessons.teach: A workload monitoring strategy is a deliberate plan for which signals you collect from a running workload, how often you look at them, and what response each signal triggers. A resource health check is one specific signal: an automatic test that asks a component a simple question, such as whether an endpoint answers correctly, and records it as healthy or unhealthy. A metric is a number sampled over time, such as error count or CPU use. An alarm is a rule that watches a metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold for a set number of periods.   Why it works: a health check answers whether a piece is alive right now, cheaply. Metrics and alarms show trends and gradual decline that a yes-or-no check misses. A strong design uses both and ties each signal to an action, such as taking a bad server out of traffic or paging someone.   Worked example: three web servers sit behind a load balancer that requests the path /health every 10 seconds. Step 1: a server returns success, so it stays in rotation. Step 2: that server's database connection pool is exhausted, but /health still succeeds because it only checks that the process is running. Step 3: the server's count of failed responses rises to 8 percent of requests, and an alarm fires after three consecutive one-minute periods above 2 percent. Step 4: a responder investigates. The health check missed the failure; the error metric caught it.   Common mistake: treating missing data as healthy. If the agent that reports metrics stops, many alarms stay in their last state or show insufficient data, so a dead monitor looks quiet. Decide deliberately how missing data is treated, and alarm on the absence of expected reports.   Consequence: a shallow health check keeps a broken server in rotation, so users see errors while the dashboard still shows green. Monitoring is only as good as the questions it asks of the system.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs five worker containers that pull jobs from a managed message queue. Each container has a health endpoint that returns success whenever its process is running. Last week one container kept its process alive but stopped taking jobs, so the queue backlog grew while its health endpoint stayed green. The team's fix has four steps. Step 1: keep the health endpoint, since it answers cheaply. Step 2: add a metric that counts failed jobs per container. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the on-call engineer is paged and removes the stuck container from the pool. Which completion correctly fills step 3?
choices: They raise the health endpoint timeout to sixty seconds so that slow containers keep receiving jobs without being flagged.
They alarm on the failed-job metric once it stays over threshold for consecutive periods.
They lower the queue retention period so that old messages are discarded sooner.
They delete the health endpoint and rely on the queue's own retry timers.
questions.why: An alarm is the rule that turns a metric into a state change once it crosses a threshold for a set number of periods, which is the link that makes step 4 happen.

questions.prompt: A team's dashboard shows every server green, yet users report errors. Which explanation best fits the idea of a health check as described in the teaching?
choices: The load balancer is designed to ignore health checks whenever traffic is heavy.
Alarms always fire before health checks do, so the green status is expected.
The metrics are sampled too rarely to be trusted at all, so the dashboard should be ignored.
The health check only confirms the process is running, so it misses requests that fail.
questions.why: A health check asks a simple alive-or-not question, so a server can pass it while still failing user requests, which is why metrics are needed too.

questions.prompt: An alarm on a per-minute error metric treats missing data as not breaching. The metric agent crashes at 02:00 and no data arrives for six hours. What happens, and what should the team do?
choices: Its history is wiped, so the team must restore the metric from backup before any alarm can work again.
It stays in its last state or shows insufficient data, hiding the outage, so the team should alarm on missing reports.
It fires at once because zero counts as an error for every missing minute, so no extra rule is needed.
Nothing changes, because the service treats silence as proof of health, so no extra rule is needed at all.
questions.why: Missing data does not mean healthy; a dead agent leaves the alarm quiet, so the fix is an alarm on the absence of expected reports.

questions.prompt: Which setup best catches a slow decline in response quality that a yes-or-no check would miss?
choices: An error-rate metric with an alarm over consecutive periods.
A health check that runs every 10 seconds and returns only success or failure.
A check that only asks whether the server's process started at boot time.
A single manual review of logs once a quarter by a team member.
questions.why: A metric sampled over time with an alarm on a threshold shows trends and gradual decline, which a binary health check cannot show.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a health check that only confirms a process is running is not enough for a web fleet, and name one tradeoff between alerting on health checks and alerting on metrics.
lessons.modelAnswer: A process-level health check only proves the program is running. It can pass while the server cannot reach its database, returns errors to every request, or is out of memory, so the load balancer keeps sending users to a broken box. For a fleet, I want the check to exercise something meaningful, like a dependency or a real response code, and I want metrics such as error rate and latency alarmed over several periods, because those show degradation. The tradeoff: a health check is quick and gives a clear yes-or-no signal that can remove a server from traffic automatically, but a deep check that calls dependencies can fail for reasons outside the server and cause a whole fleet to be removed at once. Metric alarms are slower and noisier but reveal trends and partial failures. I would use the check for automatic removal with a conservative definition, and the metrics for paging and investigation.
rubricPoints: A health check tests a specific liveness or readiness condition, so a shallow check can pass while the service is broken.
Metrics and alarms over time reveal gradual degradation and partial failures that a yes-or-no check misses.
Health checks give fast, automatic removal from traffic, but a check that depends on shared dependencies can remove the whole fleet at once.
Missing data must be handled deliberately, because a silent monitor can look like a healthy system.

suggested.rationale: Designing thresholds, evaluation periods, and missing-data behavior is best practised by building and testing alarms against simulated metric streams.

lessons.plain: Aggregating security and monitoring events means pulling the activity records from many places, such as every account, every server, every network path and every security service, into one or a few central locations where they can be searched, compared and alerted on together. Think of a building with a camera in every room. Each camera records locally, but a security desk that can see all the feeds at once is what lets someone notice that the same person tried three doors in ten minutes. Without that central view, each log is only a fragment, and the pattern that matters stays invisible. Aggregation also means keeping copies somewhere the activity cannot quietly erase, and noticing when a feed goes silent.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a company has ten cloud accounts, and an attacker makes a handful of small, unusual API calls in each one, spread over a day. Why might no single account's logs look alarming on their own, and what would make the pattern visible?
lessons.teach:
An event is one recorded action, such as a sign-in, a permission change, or a network connection. A log source is anything that produces these records, such as an account's activity trail, a virtual network's traffic records, or a security service's findings. Aggregation is the process of collecting records from many sources into a central store, where every record carries a common timestamp and an identifier for the account or machine it came from. A finding is a record a security service has already judged suspicious. Correlation means joining records from different sources to find a sequence. Retention is how long the store keeps records, and a silent source is one that has stopped sending records.

Worked example. Account A records a failed sign-in at 02:10. Account B records a new access key created at 02:40. Account C records a storage bucket policy change at 03:05. Read in isolation, each looks minor. In the central store, sorted by time, the three records sit together with their account identifiers: a failed sign-in, then a new credential in a different account, then an access change. The sequence is now visible. Step one: sort by time. Step two: group by identity or source. Step three: ask what a single actor did across all accounts.

Common mistake: assuming that turning logging on in each account is the same as aggregating it. Local logs are useful only if they reach the central store with consistent timestamps, and the central copy should be protected from the account that produced it, because a compromised account can often delete its own local records.

Consequence in a running system: if one account's feed stops, the central view shows nothing from it, and that absence looks like safety unless someone alerts on the silence.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs five accounts, and each one sends its records to one central store. An analyst pulls the records for a single afternoon. In the payments account, a role is assumed at 13:22. In the staging account, a build server opens an outbound connection at 13:25. In the logistics account, an administrator policy is attached to a role at 13:31. Worked so far: step one, the analyst sorts the three records by timestamp. Step two, the analyst groups them by the identity in each record, and the same role name appears in all three. Step three is missing. The analyst's next move, which is not yet written down, is to ask what that single actor did across every account. Which choice correctly fills in the step that is missing from the trace?
choices: Delete the local copies in the staging account so that only the central store holds the records.
Average the three timestamps so the records collapse into a single moment that can be investigated.
Pick the record with the largest amount of data in it and treat that record alone as the cause.
Ask what that single actor did across all accounts, so the sequence is read across the whole organisation rather than one account.
questions.why: After sorting by time and grouping by identity, the remaining step is to ask what one actor did across all sources, which is how the sequence becomes visible.

questions.prompt: In a central store that collects records from many sources, what does a shared timestamp format allow an analyst to do?
choices: Hide which account each record came from, so the records are anonymous.
Shorten how long each record is kept before it is removed.
Put records from different sources into one time order and read them as a sequence.
Stop the source from sending any more records until it is reviewed.
questions.why: Consistent timestamps let records from different sources be sorted together, which is what makes a cross-source sequence readable.

questions.prompt: A payroll account has sent no records to the central store for two days. The central view shows nothing at all from that account for that period. What is the right reading of this?
choices: The silence proves retention has expired, so the missing records can be ignored.
The account is safe, because a quiet source means no suspicious findings have been raised.
The account is safe, because the central store only holds records that were already judged suspicious.
The silence is a finding in itself: the source has gone silent and should trigger an alert.
questions.why: A source that has stopped sending records is a silent source, and its absence looks like safety unless someone alerts on it.

questions.prompt: A team turns on local activity logging in each of its six accounts but never forwards those logs to a central store. An attacker in one account deletes that account's local logs. Which statement best describes the gap?
choices: The logging was turned on, so the team's visibility is complete even without forwarding.
The gap is only in timestamps, so forwarding would not have helped.
The attacker can only delete logs from the central store, so the local copies were always safe.
The local logs were never aggregated, and a central copy protected from the producing account would have survived the deletion.
questions.why: Turning logging on locally is not aggregation; the central copy must reach the store and be protected from the producing account, because a compromised account can often delete its own local records.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only read logs on one server how aggregating security events across many accounts works, and name one limit or tradeoff of centralizing them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each account or server writes its own records, so on their own they show only a slice of what happened. Aggregation copies those records into one central store, with timestamps and account identifiers normalized so they can be sorted together. That lets us spot a sequence, such as a failed login in one account followed by a new access key in another. The main tradeoff is cost and concentration of risk: a central store holds a lot of sensitive data, it needs strict access control, and it adds storage and query cost as volume grows. There is also a blind spot. If a source stops sending, the central view simply has less in it, so we need an alert on missing feeds, not only on suspicious events.
rubricPoints: Explains that records from many sources are collected into one central store with common timestamps and identifiers
Gives a concrete example of a cross-account sequence that is only visible when combined
Names a tradeoff such as cost, sensitive data concentration, or access control on the central store
Notes that a silent or missing source must be alerted on, not treated as safe

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where a missing log feed across accounts must be reasoned through adds the most here, since no listed mission covers cross-account aggregation directly.

lessons.plain: Think of a building with cameras, motion sensors and a guard desk. Each sensor produces readings, and some sensors are smart enough to say this looks wrong. In a cloud account, the readings are logs (timestamped records of what happened) and metrics (numbers measured over time). Four AWS services sit on top of those readings. One watches activity and flags likely threats. One gathers logs into a single storage pool. One collects findings from many tools into one list. One hunts for sensitive data stored in buckets. Together they answer two questions: what looks abnormal, and where should I look first?
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has ten cloud accounts, and each one shows its security alerts on a different screen. Before reading on, what problem do you think one place that collects all those alerts would solve, and what might it still miss?
lessons.teach: A metric is a number tracked over time, such as failed logins per minute. A log is a timestamped record of one event, such as an API call. A finding is a service's conclusion that something is suspicious or non-compliant, usually with a severity level. An alert is a notification fired when a rule matches. A dashboard is a view that shows these numbers together. Amazon GuardDuty is a managed threat detector: it reads account activity such as API calls, network flow and DNS lookups, compares them with normal behaviour, and produces findings without you installing agents. Amazon Security Lake is a managed data lake: it collects logs from many sources into object storage in one shared open schema so several tools can query the same data. AWS Security Hub is an aggregator: it gathers findings from many services into one format and checks the account against compliance standards. Amazon Macie scans object storage for sensitive data, such as personal identifiers, and reports where it is and who can reach it. Worked example: an access key is used from an unfamiliar country at 3 am. Step 1: the activity log records the API calls. Step 2: GuardDuty compares them with the account's normal pattern and raises a high-severity finding. Step 3: Security Hub receives that finding beside its compliance results. Step 4: an alert rule on high-severity findings notifies the on-call engineer. Step 5: the analyst queries the Security Lake history to see what else that key did. Common mistake: treating a quiet dashboard as proof of safety. If a log source is switched off, these services see nothing and produce no finding. A missing log is itself a finding, and it means an attacker could operate for weeks without anyone noticing.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a staging account with a storage bucket named promo-uploads. Step 1: Amazon Macie scans the bucket and reports that 1,200 objects contain payment card numbers. Step 2: Macie's report shows the bucket grants read access to anyone on the internet. Step 3: AWS Security Hub receives the Macie finding beside its own compliance results and marks the account as failing one control. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: the team re-runs the Macie scan, confirms the bucket is no longer reachable from the internet, and the finding closes. Which action fills step 4?
choices: Macie deletes the 1,200 objects automatically, so the team only needs to wait for the next scheduled scan.
Security Hub suppresses the failing control, which stops the result from appearing again.
GuardDuty recalculates the account's normal pattern so the bucket is treated as expected behaviour.
The team removes the public read grant so that only the intended internal roles can reach the objects.
questions.why: Macie reports where sensitive data is and who can reach it but does not change permissions, so a person must restrict the public grant before the rescan can show the exposure has closed.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the difference between a log and a metric?
choices: A metric is a service's conclusion that something is suspicious, and a log is the notification the team receives about it.
A log is one timestamped event record; a metric is a number tracked over time.
A log is a number tracked over time, and a metric is a single record of one event, so the two terms swap meanings.
Logs and metrics are the same data, and the words only differ by which cloud service produced them.
questions.why: A log records one timestamped event such as an API call, while a metric is a number followed over time such as failed logins per minute.

questions.prompt: A new account shows zero GuardDuty findings and a clean Security Hub score. The team later learns that the log feed GuardDuty reads was switched off in one region months ago. What is the right conclusion?
choices: Zero findings is normal for a new account, so no action is needed until the first finding appears.
The account is safe, since GuardDuty only reports findings from regions where the account has recent activity.
The clean result proves nothing; the switched-off feed is itself a finding to fix.
Security Hub would have recalculated its score to exclude the switched-off feed, so the clean result stands.
questions.why: If a log source is off, the services see nothing and produce no finding, so the silence reflects a gap in coverage rather than safety, and the gap should be fixed.

questions.prompt: Which service finds where personal identifiers such as names and national ID numbers sit inside object storage, and who can reach them?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty, because it reads API calls and DNS lookups and compares them with normal behaviour.
Amazon Security Lake, because it stores logs from many sources in one shared open schema for querying.
Amazon Macie, which scans object storage for sensitive data and reports who can reach it.
AWS Security Hub, because it gathers findings from many services and checks compliance standards.
questions.why: Macie is the scanner for sensitive data in object storage and reports both the location of the data and the access paths to it, while the other three services do not scan stored content.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we turned on GuardDuty, so we are covered for data exposure. Explain to them what each of these four services does, where its inputs come from, and one limit they should not rely on.
lessons.modelAnswer: GuardDuty is a threat detector. It reads account activity like API calls, network flow and DNS, and raises findings when behaviour looks unusual or malicious. Security Lake is a storage layer that gathers logs from many sources into one open format so they can be searched together and kept for investigations. Security Hub is the aggregator: it pulls findings from GuardDuty, Macie and other tools into one list and checks the account against compliance standards. Macie is the one that addresses data exposure. It scans S3 buckets for sensitive data and reports which buckets hold it and who can read them. So GuardDuty alone does not cover data exposure. The limit to remember is that every one of these depends on logs being enabled and on the right sources feeding in. A disabled source produces silence, not safety.
rubricPoints: GuardDuty detects threats from account activity and produces findings without agents
Security Lake stores logs from many sources in one shared format for querying
Security Hub aggregates findings and checks compliance, but does not detect threats itself
Macie is the service that finds sensitive data exposed in storage
Missing or disabled log sources mean silent gaps, so coverage must be verified

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks a learner through these four services' roles and how their findings connect, so reading the service summaries is the best fit.

lessons.plain: This objective is about making security checks repeat on their own instead of being done by hand once and forgotten. Think of a building inspector who checks every floor each night, writes down anything out of code, and sends the list to one shared inbox, while a maintenance crew quietly fixes the small things that drift back. In the cloud, the inspector is a set of recorded configuration rules, the inbox is a central findings list, and the crew is a scheduled routine that keeps machines set the way you intended. The skill is wiring these three together so problems are found, recorded and acted on without anyone having to remember to look.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a security setting on a server was correct on Monday and someone changed it on Tuesday with nobody noticing, what would have to be running for your team to learn about the change by Wednesday morning, and who would act on it?
lessons.teach:
A configuration is the set of settings that describe a resource, such as whether a storage bucket is private or whether a server has a particular agent installed. Drift is what happens when the real setting moves away from the one you intended. Automating assessment means checking that continuously or on a schedule instead of relying on a person to remember.

AWS Config is the recording service. It keeps a history of each resource's configuration and runs rules, which are checks that mark each resource as compliant or noncompliant. A conformance pack is a packaged bundle of many such rules, often with remediation actions attached, deployed together as one unit to an account or across an organization. This applies one standard everywhere with identical content.

Security Hub is the aggregator. It collects findings from Config, threat detection services and other sources into one list, puts them in a common format so they can be compared, and scores your accounts against chosen security standards. A responder usually starts there.

Systems Manager State Manager is the keeper. You declare a desired state, such as an agent installed or a setting applied, and it runs a predefined document on a schedule against managed instances, reapplying it when drift appears.

Worked example: a rule checks that public access is blocked on a bucket. On Tuesday at 10:00 someone turns that protection off. Config records the change and the rule marks the bucket noncompliant. Security Hub receives the noncompliant result as a finding with a severity. A responder, or an automated remediation, restores the setting, and the next evaluation records the bucket as compliant again.

Common mistake: treating a clean compliance score as proof of safety. If recording is switched off for a resource type, or a conformance pack was never deployed to a newly created account, that resource is not assessed at all, and the dashboard can still look green. Missing coverage is itself a gap that must be found and closed.

The pipeline is only as strong as its coverage. A pack deployed to some accounts but not others leaves the rest silently unmonitored.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight runs 25 servers. Its Systems Manager State Manager setup (a declared desired state, which State Manager calls an association, that runs a predefined document on a schedule) requires a log shipping agent to be installed and running on every server, and runs every 4 hours. Here is the sequence. Step 1: at 09:15 an operator stops the agent on server NF-14. Step 2: the next scheduled run is at 12:00. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the next compliance report shows NF-14 as having the agent running. Which step 3 completes the sequence?
choices: The document runs on NF-14 at 12:00, reinstalls and starts the agent, and returns the server to the declared state.
Security Hub closes the NF-14 finding at 09:15 without any run taking place.
AWS Config deletes NF-14's configuration history so the old stopped state is forgotten.
State Manager disables the association until a person approves the manual change.
questions.why: State Manager reapplies its document on each scheduled run, so at 12:00 the agent is restored, which is what makes step 4 possible.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a conformance pack in AWS Config?
choices: A packaged bundle of many rules, often with remediation actions attached, deployed together as one unit.
A schedule that reruns a predefined document on managed instances.
A single rule that checks one resource type in one account.
A dashboard that scores each account against a chosen security standard.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a conformance pack as a packaged bundle of many rules deployed together as one unit, which is the third choice.

questions.prompt: A company has six AWS accounts and deployed its conformance pack to five of them. The sixth account was created last week and has never received the pack. Security Hub shows no findings for it, and the team's summary says all accounts look healthy. What is the right way to read that summary?
choices: Security Hub assesses every new account automatically, so the empty list confirms the account is clean.
Findings for a new account only appear after a 30-day warm-up, so zero findings is normal at this stage.
The sixth account is compliant because it is newer and usually has fewer resources to misconfigure.
There is a coverage gap: nothing in the sixth account is evaluated, so the empty results say nothing about its safety.
questions.why: A resource that is not assessed produces no finding, so silence in an unmonitored account is a missing-coverage gap that must be found and closed.

questions.prompt: A State Manager association runs every 2 hours and keeps a time synchronisation setting applied on a host. At 10:05 someone changes that setting by hand, and the next scheduled run is at 12:00. For how long is the host out of its declared state, and what would narrow that window?
choices: Only until 10:06, because State Manager watches for changes and corrects them immediately.
Until the security team reviews the dashboard manually the following Monday.
Indefinitely, because State Manager applies its document only once when the association is created.
Until 12:00, about one hour and fifty-five minutes; a shorter schedule interval narrows the gap.
questions.why: State Manager reapplies the declared state on each scheduled run, so drift persists until the next run, and running the schedule more often shrinks that period.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Config, Security Hub and Systems Manager State Manager divide the work of keeping an account in its intended state, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on automated checks.
lessons.modelAnswer: Config records what each resource looks like and evaluates it against rules, so it answers whether something is compliant. Security Hub gathers those results and other security findings into one list, so the team has a single place to triage. State Manager is the enforcer: it runs a defined routine on a schedule to push managed instances back to the state we declared. Together they cover detection, consolidation and correction. The main limit is coverage. These tools only check what is recorded, enrolled and in scope, so a resource type with recording off, or an account missing a pack, is invisible and can look healthy. Automated remediation also carries risk: a fix that runs too broadly or on a wrong assumption can break a working service, so teams should test remediations and review what they change.
rubricPoints: Config records resource configuration and evaluates rules for compliance
Security Hub aggregates findings from several sources into one place to triage
State Manager runs a defined routine on a schedule to correct drift on managed instances
A tradeoff or limit is named, such as coverage gaps or the risk of automated fixes

suggested.rationale: A scenario where a setting drifts and the learner must trace which service detects, records and corrects it adds the most to the wiring skill, and no listed mission covers these AWS services.

lessons.plain: A log source is anything that writes down what happened: a record of who changed a setting, which network connection was opened, or which name was looked up. Storage is the place those records are kept. Identifying them means asking two questions before anything is switched on: what must we be able to answer later, and what could an attacker do to hide the evidence? A good answer names the records needed for each question, the place they are kept, how long they stay, who may read them, and whether they can be altered. Because an attack that leaves no record is hard to investigate, a missing expected log is itself a finding worth fixing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Six months from now, someone asks who deleted a storage bucket in one of your forty accounts. Where would you want that answer to come from, and what would stop an attacker with admin rights in that one account from erasing the answer?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A log source is a producer of event records, such as an account-wide record of API activity, a network traffic log, or a DNS resolver query log. A storage destination is where those records are delivered, such as an object storage bucket or a managed log group. Retention is how long records are kept. Tamper resistance means a person holding admin rights in a workload account cannot erase or rewrite the records.

The method is to start from requirements, not from the tool. Requirements usually cover what must be visible (control-plane actions, traffic between subnets, name lookups), how long evidence must last, who must be able to read it, and how it must be protected. Each requirement then maps to a source and a destination. Control-plane activity is recorded by an organization-wide CloudTrail trail. Network traffic metadata comes from VPC flow logs or transit gateway flow logs. Name lookups come from Route 53 Resolver query logs, because flow logs show connections, not the names looked up.

Worked example. Requirement: one year of API history for forty accounts, readable by the security team, and not erasable by an admin in a workload account. Step 1: create one organization trail in the management account, covering all regions and all member accounts, including accounts created later. Step 2: deliver it to a bucket in a separate log archive account. Step 3: turn on versioning and object lock in retention mode so records cannot be deleted before the period ends. Step 4: move older objects to a cheaper storage class after 90 days and expire them after 365. Step 5: grant read access only in the archive account, to the security team.

Common mistake: delivering logs to a bucket in the same account as the workload, where whoever compromised that account can delete the evidence. Consequence: an attacker who stops a trail leaves no trace unless an alert fires on the stop action itself, so a disabled trail is a missing log that must be detected.

questions.prompt: A payments team runs one VPC with six subnets. Requirement: keep network traffic metadata for 120 days, readable only by a security team in a separate audit account, and not erasable by an administrator in the payments account. Step 1: enable VPC flow logs on the VPC, since flow logs record connections between subnets. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: set object lock in retention mode with a 120-day period on the destination bucket. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Deliver the flow logs to a bucket in the separate audit account, so the admin in the payments account cannot reach the evidence
Deliver the flow logs to a log group inside the payments account so the payments team can query them directly
Enable Route 53 Resolver query logging in the payments account so name lookups are also captured
Set a lifecycle rule that expires the flow log objects after 30 days to reduce storage cost
questions.why: Delivering the records to a bucket in a separate account keeps them out of reach of an administrator in the workload account, which is what the tamper-resistance requirement demands.

questions.prompt: A security lead needs records showing which hostnames instances in a private subnet looked up during the last 30 days. Which log source produces that evidence?
choices: Organization-wide CloudTrail trail
Object storage access logs for the archive bucket
Route 53 Resolver query logs
VPC flow logs
questions.why: Name lookups are captured by resolver query logs, because flow logs only show connections between addresses and not the names that were resolved.

questions.prompt: An attacker with admin rights in a workload account stops the account's only trail and then deletes the stored log objects, which sit in a bucket in that same account. What is the main lesson for the design?
choices: Turn on flow logs so the connections the attacker made are still visible
Keep the trail running and rely on the attacker not knowing the bucket name
Deliver the logs to a separate archive account and alert on the stop-trail action itself, because a disabled trail is a missing log that must be detected
Increase the retention period so more history exists before the deletion
questions.why: Storing evidence outside the compromised account protects it from deletion, and an alert on the stop action reveals the gap, since a silent disabled trail leaves no record.

questions.prompt: A team's requirement says its logs must be tamper resistant. Which statement correctly describes what that means?
choices: An admin in the account that produced the records cannot erase or rewrite them
The logs are compressed and encrypted so that they take less space on disk
The logs are copied to a second region so a regional outage cannot destroy them
Logs are deleted automatically after the retention period ends so storage does not grow
questions.why: Tamper resistance means that someone holding admin rights in the workload account is unable to erase or rewrite the records, which is a different property from compression, replication, or expiry.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which log sources to enable and where to store them for a new account. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from what we must be able to answer later: who changed what, what traffic left the network, which names were looked up. Each question maps to a source. The organization trail covers API activity, flow logs cover network connection metadata, and resolver query logs cover DNS names, because flow logs do not show which names were resolved. Then I choose storage from the requirements: a central archive account that workload admins cannot write to or delete from, versioning and object lock for retention, lifecycle rules that move older data to cheaper storage, and read access limited to the security team. The main tradeoff is cost against query speed. Keeping everything in a central bucket for a long time is cheap per gigabyte but large in volume, and searching raw archived data is slower than a live index, so I keep recent data searchable and push older data to the archive.
rubricPoints: Starts from the questions the logs must answer, not from the tool.
Maps each need to a specific source, such as API activity, network metadata, or DNS names.
Chooses a destination that workload admins cannot erase, with retention and restricted read access.
Names a real tradeoff, such as storage cost against query speed or log volume.

suggested.rationale: Choosing sources and storage against competing requirements is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which none of the listed missions covers directly.

lessons.plain: Logging in a cloud account means keeping a diary of what happened: who called which service, when, and from where, plus what the servers themselves wrote down. This objective is about setting that diary up correctly across many accounts at once. You create one organization-wide record of account activity, send those records to a separate account that only the security team controls, and install a small agent on servers so their own log files get shipped too. If any piece is missing, the gap is itself a finding, because you cannot investigate what was never recorded.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has 40 cloud accounts, and an incident happened in one of them last month. What would you need to have set up beforehand so you could answer 'who did what, and when' for every account? Why would it be a problem if the records lived only inside the account that was attacked?
lessons.teach:
CloudTrail is the AWS service that records API calls: every request made to the cloud control plane, such as creating a server, changing a permission, or deleting a bucket. A trail is the configuration that tells CloudTrail to deliver those records to storage. An organization trail is created once in the management account of an AWS Organization and covers every member account, including accounts created later. Its records usually go to an S3 bucket, which is object storage, and can also go to a CloudWatch Logs log group, which is a managed store you can search and alarm on. A dedicated logging account is a separate account whose only job is holding these archives. Workload accounts can write to it but cannot edit or delete what is there, so an attacker who takes over a workload account cannot erase their own tracks. The CloudWatch agent is software on a virtual machine that reads chosen files, such as a web server access log, and ships new lines to CloudWatch Logs. It is configured by a file that names each log file and its destination, and it needs permission, granted through the instance's role, to write.

Worked example: the management account creates an organization trail covering all regions, delivering to a bucket in the logging account. A new account joins the organization; the trail covers it automatically, so its activity lands in the same bucket. A web server in a workload account runs the agent, whose configuration names the nginx access log; the instance role lets it write, and the lines appear in a log group in the logging account.

Common mistake: creating a separate trail in each account, so new accounts are missed, or keeping the only copy inside the workload account where an attacker can delete it. The consequence is that the evidence disappears exactly when you need it. A central, write-only archive keeps the record intact.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a Linux virtual machine in its fraud account that scores card transactions. The scoring program writes alerts to /opt/scorer/logs/alerts.log. The engineer wants those alert lines searchable in CloudWatch Logs under a log group named /fraud/alerts. Steps: (1) write the agent configuration file naming /opt/scorer/logs/alerts.log and the destination log group /fraud/alerts; (2) start the agent; (3) confirm the lines appear. The engineer did steps 1 and 2, but no lines reach the log group. The agent is running and the file is growing. The one step that was never done is the one that gives the virtual machine permission to write to CloudWatch Logs. Which action completes the setup?
choices: Attach an instance role that grants permission to write to CloudWatch Logs
Enable versioning on the scorer's local disk so old lines are kept
Create a second trail in the fraud account that delivers to the same log group
Rename alerts.log so the agent picks up a fresh file
questions.why: The agent needs permission, granted through the instance's role, before it can ship new lines, and that permission is the missing step here.

questions.prompt: What does an organization trail cover, and why does that matter for a company that creates new accounts every quarter?
choices: Only the management account, with member accounts reporting to it by manual export
Every member account of the organization, including accounts created later, so new activity is captured without extra setup
Only the accounts that existed when the trail was created, so each new account needs its own trail
Only the regions the engineer selects in each individual account
questions.why: An organization trail is created once in the management account and automatically covers every member account, including ones added later.

questions.prompt: A workload account is compromised and the attacker tries to delete the CloudTrail records stored in that same account. Why is a write-only archive in a separate logging account the better design?
choices: Workload accounts can write to the archive but cannot edit or delete what is already stored there, so the attacker cannot erase their own activity
Separate accounts automatically encrypt records with a key the attacker cannot see
The logging account is faster at answering queries than the workload account
The workload account is billed for storage, so records are cheaper to delete there
questions.why: Keeping the only copy inside a compromised workload account lets the attacker remove evidence, while a write-only logging account keeps the record intact.

questions.prompt: An engineer sets up the CloudWatch agent on a web server. The agent's configuration file names the nginx access log and its destination log group. Which statement correctly describes what the agent does?
choices: It reads the nginx access log and sends new lines to CloudWatch Logs, using the instance's role to authorize the writes
It copies the entire operating system disk to CloudWatch Logs every hour
It sends the log to the logging account's bucket directly without any configuration file
It replaces nginx's own logging so the server no longer writes an access log to disk
questions.why: The agent is software that reads the chosen files, ships new lines to CloudWatch Logs as named in its configuration, and needs role permission to write.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we send the organization's CloudTrail records to a dedicated logging account instead of keeping them in each workload account, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: We keep the records in a separate logging account so that a compromise of a workload account cannot erase the evidence of what the attacker did. Workload teams can write their logs there, but they cannot delete or change the archive, and the security team holds the only permission to manage it. An organization trail also means new accounts are covered without someone remembering to set up logging for them. The tradeoff is operational. Investigators now need access to a different account, which means cross-account roles and a clear process for requesting them, and the central bucket and its log group can become costly to store and query at scale. Someone also has to own the lifecycle rules, so old records are retained for the required period and then removed deliberately.
rubricPoints: Explains that a separate account with restricted write access protects evidence from a compromised workload account.
Explains that an organization trail covers all member accounts, including new ones.
Names a real tradeoff such as cross-account access for investigators or storage cost and retention management.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly console configuration, product behaviour and account structure facts, which a reference read covers better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Think of a security data lake as one big, organized storage room where security logs from many places get dropped in the same format, so you can search across all of them at once. Amazon Security Lake is a managed service that collects security logs from many accounts and regions into one storage location you own, converts them into a shared standard layout, and lets approved tools read them. The point is that when something goes wrong, you do not have to hunt through a dozen log formats in a dozen places.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company has logs from five AWS accounts, each stored in its own bucket in its own format, what would make a security investigation slow, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Security Lake is a managed service that gathers security-relevant logs and findings into a data lake, meaning a central storage area built on Amazon S3 object storage that holds data in its raw or lightly processed form. Security Lake stores the data in an open standard called the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF), a shared layout for fields such as the account, the time, the actor and the action, so a login event from one source looks similar to a network event from another. Data is kept in a columnar file format, which lets query tools read only the columns they need.

Why it works: once logs share one schema and one location, a single query can ask who touched a resource across every account, and tools built for the schema can read it without custom parsing. Security Lake can ingest AWS sources such as CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs, Route 53 Resolver query logs, and Security Hub findings. Custom sources can be added if you convert them to the same schema. Sources are enabled per region, and an administrator account can set this up for an entire organization.

Third-party integration works through subscribers. A subscriber is an account or outside tool that you grant read access to a chosen set of sources. Access can be direct, through query engines reading the underlying S3 data, or through notifications that tell the subscriber when new data arrives, so a third-party security information and event management tool can pull it on its own schedule.

Worked example: a team enables CloudTrail and VPC flow logs in a security account. Security Lake writes both into the lake in OCSF. An analyst grants a SIEM subscriber read access to only those two sources. When a new batch lands, the notification tells the SIEM to pull it, and a later investigation query filters by account ID across both sources.

Common mistake: assuming Security Lake replaces collection for every source. Unsupported sources still need their own pipeline, and a source not enabled in a region leaves a gap that looks like silence.

Consequence: a missing source is itself a finding. An absent flow log means the lake is quiet about that network path, not that the path is safe.

Security Lake turns scattered security evidence into one searchable, shared, standardized record.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs its checkout workloads in two regions, eu-central-1 and us-west-2. Its security team enables Amazon Security Lake and turns on Route 53 Resolver query logs in eu-central-1 only. Step 1: they confirm the eu-central-1 DNS logs land in the lake in the OCSF schema. Step 2: they grant a log-analytics subscriber read access to the Route 53 Resolver query log source. Step 3 is missing. Later, an analyst searches the lake for DNS queries from the us-west-2 checkout workloads and finds no rows at all. Which missing step explains this?
choices: Enable the Route 53 Resolver query log source in us-west-2 as well, because sources are switched on per region.
Add a custom source for the us-west-2 workloads, because the lake only accepts DNS records from one region.
Ask the subscriber to request a backfill of older DNS queries from the us-west-2 region.
Convert the DNS logs to a columnar file format before any subscriber is allowed to read them.
questions.why: Sources are enabled per region, so a region left off produces no records, and the empty search result is a gap rather than evidence of no DNS activity.

questions.prompt: What does the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) give a Security Lake data set?
choices: A shared field layout, so a login from one source and a network event from another use similar names for account, time, actor and action.
A permission model that limits which accounts may read each source, applied uniformly to every subscriber.
A proprietary compression method that shrinks each log file before it is written to the S3 bucket for storage.
A rule set that decides which alerts a third-party SIEM should raise on each incoming batch of records.
questions.why: OCSF is an open shared layout for common fields, which is what lets events from different sources be queried together.

questions.prompt: A team has an in-house application that writes access logs in its own custom text format. They enable Security Lake and assume the application's logs will appear in the lake automatically. Which statement is correct?
choices: They appear automatically, because the lake reads any log file that lands in its S3 bucket.
They do not appear on their own; they need a separate pipeline that converts them to the shared schema.
They appear automatically once the account joins an organization that has an administrator account.
They appear only after a subscriber requests them, and then only in that subscriber's region.
questions.why: Security Lake does not replace collection for unsupported sources, so custom logs need their own pipeline and conversion to the shared schema before they show up.

questions.prompt: A third-party SIEM should pull new security data on its own schedule instead of querying the lake live every time. Which access arrangement fits this need?
choices: A public S3 bucket so the SIEM can fetch objects at any time without holding any credentials.
Notifications that tell the subscriber when new data arrives, so it pulls the batch on its own schedule.
Write access to the S3 bucket so the SIEM can copy files into its own storage whenever it chooses.
Direct read access through a query engine that reads the underlying S3 data on every request, with no notifications configured.
questions.why: Subscriber notifications signal new data arrival so an outside tool can pull on its own timing, which is the arrangement the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon Security Lake does, how a third-party security tool gets access to its data, and one limit or tradeoff of centralizing logs this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Security Lake collects our security logs, like CloudTrail management events and VPC flow logs, from accounts and regions into one S3-based store, and converts them into the OCSF shared schema so they can be queried together. A third-party SIEM does not get a copy by default. We add it as a subscriber, scoped to specific sources, and it either reads through a query engine or gets notified when new data lands and pulls it. The tradeoff is that the lake is only as complete as its enabled sources. Anything unsupported or not enabled in a region is missing, and that silence can look like safety, so we track source coverage as its own check. Centralizing also concentrates sensitive data, so access to the bucket and subscriber grants need tight control and regular review.
rubricPoints: Security Lake stores normalized security logs in a central S3-based data lake.
Data is converted to the OCSF shared schema so different sources can be queried together.
Third-party tools receive scoped subscriber access rather than a full copy of everything.
Coverage gaps from unenabled or unsupported sources look like silence and must be tracked as findings.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and console setup, which reading covers better than any currently listed or planned mission.

lessons.plain: Security logs are records of what happened in a cloud account: who signed in, which systems talked to which, and what changed. Collecting them is only half the job, because you also need to ask them questions quickly, such as which accounts failed to sign in at night or which security alerts are still open. This objective covers three tools for asking those questions. One searches recent log streams with a query language, one runs SQL over large archived log files sitting in storage, and one gathers security findings from many services into a single list you can filter. Knowing which tool fits which question is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a million log lines from last week and need to know which user accounts failed to sign in more than 50 times. Would you scan the lines by hand, write a small program, or use a query tool? What would the tool need to do first before it could answer?
lessons.teach:
Three tools cover most log questions on AWS, and each reads data from a different place. CloudWatch Logs Insights is an interactive query tool for log groups, which are named collections of log streams held in CloudWatch Logs, the service that stores logs from applications and AWS services. You write a short pipeline: choose a time range, filter the lines, then aggregate them, for example by counting per user name. Amazon Athena is a serverless SQL service. It runs standard SQL directly over data files kept in Amazon S3 object storage, using a table definition that maps those files to named columns. You pay for the bytes each query scans, so narrowing by date partition matters. AWS Security Hub collects findings, which are standardized records of a security issue such as a publicly exposed resource or a failed configuration check, from many services into one list with severity and status fields.

Why it works: each tool suits a different shape of question. Logs Insights answers fast, recent, exploratory questions. Athena answers large historical questions across months of archived logs. Security Hub answers which known issues are open and how serious they are.

Worked example: you want to know which user names had more than 20 failed console sign-ins last night. In Logs Insights you set the time range to last night, filter for failed sign-in events, count the results grouped by user name, and sort the counts from highest to lowest. Step one limits the data, step two keeps only relevant lines, step three groups them, and step four ranks them.

Common mistake: treating an empty result as proof that nothing happened. If the trail or log group was not switched on for that account or region, the query returns nothing even when attacks occurred. Check coverage before trusting a quiet answer.

Consequence: a missing log source makes every later query silently incomplete, so a gap in logging is itself a finding that must be fixed.

questions.prompt: A small security team keeps a year of load balancer access logs as compressed files in an S3 bucket, organized into folders by year, month, and day. They want to know which client IP addresses received the most HTTP 403 (forbidden) responses on the 14th of February. Their Athena workflow is: step 1, limit the query to the February 14 folder so only that day's files are scanned; step 2, keep only rows where the status code is 403; step 3, [missing]; step 4, sort the counts from highest to lowest. Which step 3 completes the workflow?
choices: Check that the log retention period on the bucket is at least ninety days
Export the filtered rows to a spreadsheet and count the client IP addresses by hand
Run the same query again over the whole bucket with no date limit so the counts are more complete
Group the filtered rows by client IP address and count the rows in each group
questions.why: Grouping by the field of interest and counting each group is the aggregation step that turns filtered lines into per-IP totals, which the sort in step 4 then ranks.

questions.prompt: A company has eighteen months of archived application logs stored as data files in Amazon S3. An engineer needs to run standard SQL over those files, using a table definition that maps the files to named columns, and pays only for the bytes each query scans. Which tool fits this need?
choices: Amazon Athena, a serverless SQL service that queries data files in S3 directly
AWS Security Hub, a list of standardized security findings with severity and status
An Amazon S3 lifecycle rule that moves older objects into a cheaper storage class
CloudWatch Logs Insights, a query tool for log groups held in CloudWatch Logs
questions.why: Athena is the serverless SQL service that reads files in S3 through a table definition and charges by bytes scanned, which matches large historical questions over archived files.

questions.prompt: On a Monday at 9 a.m., an analyst runs a Logs Insights query over the last twelve hours for failed sign-in events in a log group. The query returns zero rows, and the analyst concludes that no attacks happened overnight. What is the most important mistake in this reasoning?
choices: The analyst should have used Athena instead, because Athena always returns complete results
The time range should have been set to the full calendar year before any conclusion is drawn
The analyst never checked whether the log group was receiving data from that account and region, so the empty result may reflect missing coverage rather than no activity
Logs Insights cannot filter by event type, so the zero result is meaningless
questions.why: An empty result only means something if the log source was switched on for that account or region, so coverage must be verified before trusting a quiet answer.

questions.prompt: A security manager wants a single list of all open findings rated high or critical severity across the services in one AWS account, so the team can see which known issues still need work. Which tool and reason best match this request?
choices: CloudWatch Logs Insights, because it aggregates by user name and sorts counts
Athena, because it can scan archived logs and rank results by severity field value
Security Hub, because it collects standardized findings from many services into one list with severity and status fields
A log group retention setting, because it controls which findings are kept for review
questions.why: Security Hub is designed to show which known issues are open and how serious they are, by gathering standardized findings into one list with severity and status fields.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks when you would use CloudWatch Logs Insights, Amazon Athena, or Security Hub for a security question. In your own words, explain how you would choose between them, and name one limit or tradeoff of the tool you would reach for first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the question covers. If it concerns the last few hours and I need to explore interactively, I would use CloudWatch Logs Insights, since it queries log groups quickly and I can refine the filter as I go. If the question spans months of archived logs stored in S3, I would use Athena, because it scans the files in place without loading them anywhere. It bills by data scanned, though, so I would narrow the date partitions first and watch the cost. If the question is which known security issues are open and how severe they are, I would go to Security Hub, which consolidates findings from many services. The tradeoff to name is coverage: each tool only shows what was actually logged into it. A quiet result can mean logging was never turned on, so I would confirm the source before trusting the answer.
rubricPoints: Matches the tool to the question: recent interactive logs, historical archives in storage, or consolidated open findings.
Explains that Athena runs SQL over files in storage and charges by the data scanned.
States that a query can only return logs that were actually collected, so empty results need checking.
Mentions narrowing the time range or date partitions to keep queries fast and cheap.

suggested.rationale: Athena and Logs Insights both ask questions of log data in a query language, so practising SQL-style questions on a sample log set builds this skill most directly.

lessons.plain: Logs from many systems arrive in different shapes: one writes the timestamp first, another writes a JSON object, another a line of plain text. Normalizing means converting them all into one common set of field names. Parsing means pulling individual fields out of raw text. Correlating means joining events from different sources that share a key, such as a user name or IP address, so a trail of small events tells one story. Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search and analytics engine that stores and queries these records. AWS Lambda is a small function that runs on demand to transform them. Amazon Managed Grafana is a hosted dashboard tool that charts the results. Together they turn noise into something a person can investigate.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two systems log the same failed login. One writes 'user=alice ip=10.0.0.5 result=fail' and the other writes 'Failed login for alice from 10.0.0.5'. Why would a search for failed logins miss the second one unless something changes first?
lessons.teach:
A log record is one line or object describing something that happened. Parsing is reading a raw record and extracting named fields such as source address, user, outcome and time. Normalizing is mapping those fields onto one shared schema, so a failed login from a firewall and one from an application both store the source address in the same field. Correlating is joining normalized events that share a key, such as an address or session identifier, across sources within a time window, so that many small events reveal one incident.

Why it works: a search engine can only answer questions about fields it has indexed. Raw text is hard to filter, but once every event has a timestamp, an actor and an outcome as separate fields, one query can count failures per address per minute. In this stack, a Lambda function runs when new records arrive, does the parsing and renaming, and writes the normalized document into an OpenSearch index. Managed Grafana then queries that index and draws the time series and tables.

Worked example: a raw line reads 'Mar 3 10:14:02 web1 sshd: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.9'. Step one, parse: extract timestamp 10:14:02, host web1, service sshd, outcome failed, user admin, source 203.0.113.9. Step two, normalize: store outcome as failure, user name as admin, source address as 203.0.113.9, and convert the timestamp to UTC. Step three, correlate: count documents with that source address and failure outcome in five minutes; if the count passes twenty, a Grafana panel alert fires.

Common mistake: normalizing and discarding the original raw line, so when a parser turns out to be wrong, the evidence is gone. A second mistake is trusting local timestamps without converting them, which puts events from two sources in the wrong order.

Consequence in a running system: if the Lambda fails quietly and writes nothing, the dashboard shows a calm period that looks like safety. A gap in ingestion is itself a signal, so ingestion volume needs its own alert.

questions.prompt: Halvard Logistics sends two log sources into the same pipeline. Its VPN gateway writes local time with an offset, and its cloud sign-in service writes UTC. A VPN line reads: 2024-05-12 22:40:11 +02:00 vpn-gw2 rejected login user=j.okafor src=198.51.100.44. The team's trace shows: Step one, parse: time 22:40:11 with offset +02:00, user j.okafor, outcome rejected, source 198.51.100.44. Step two, normalize: outcome becomes failure, user becomes user name, source becomes source address. Step three, correlate: count events with source address 198.51.100.44 and outcome failure within 10 minutes, and alert above 15. The trace skips one step that is needed before correlation can be trusted. Which step is missing?
choices: Delete the raw VPN line once the fields are normalized, to keep the index small
Convert the timestamp to UTC so that VPN events sort correctly against the UTC cloud sign-in events
Raise the alert threshold to 50 failures so that busy office mornings do not cause false alarms
Rename the source address field to ip_address so that Grafana can chart it as a numeric value
questions.why: Correlation across sources depends on a shared time basis, so the local-offset timestamp must be converted to UTC before events from the two sources are joined and ordered.

questions.prompt: In a log pipeline, what does it mean to correlate events?
choices: Keeping the original raw text of each record alongside its extracted fields
Renaming fields from each source so that they all use the same names
Splitting one long log line into separate named fields such as user and outcome
Joining normalized events that share a key, such as an address or session identifier, across sources within a time window
questions.why: Correlating means linking events that share a key across sources inside a time window so that many small events can be read together as one incident.

questions.prompt: A company called Pemberton Dental has a perimeter firewall whose logs name the client address src_ip, and a patient portal whose logs name it client_address. The team wants one query that counts failed logins from a single address across both sources. What is the most direct first step?
choices: Create two separate dashboards, one per source, and compare the counts by eye each morning
Map both src_ip and client_address onto one shared source address field during normalization
Store the portal logs in a separate index so that the firewall fields do not overwrite them
Increase the window to 24 hours so that the two names will eventually match in the index
questions.why: A single query can only count across sources when both sources' address values sit in the same normalized field, which is what normalizing is for.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function that parses an account's sign-in logs fails silently over a long weekend. On Monday, the Grafana failure panel shows zero failed sign-ins for the whole weekend. What is the most sound reading of that panel?
choices: The account had no failed sign-ins, so no investigation is needed
The gap is unverified, because missing ingestion looks the same as calm; ingestion volume should have its own alert
The weekend was quiet, so the alert threshold should be lowered to catch smaller attacks
The panel is wrong, so the team should delete it and rebuild it from scratch
questions.why: A silent ingestion failure produces an empty panel that looks like safety, so the gap itself needs its own monitored signal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a raw SSH failure line becomes something you can alert on in OpenSearch and Grafana. Name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A raw sshd line is just text, so first a parser pulls out the timestamp, host, user, outcome and source address as separate fields. Normalization then maps those fields onto a shared schema, so this event looks the same as a failed login from another source. The Lambda function does this and writes the document into an OpenSearch index. Grafana queries the index by source address and time window, and an alert fires when failures from one address pass a threshold. The tradeoff is that the alert is only as good as the parser: a changed log format can silently produce empty fields, so the pipeline needs its own check on ingestion volume and parse-failure counts. I would also keep the raw line stored alongside the normalized fields so we can re-parse later when the format changes.
rubricPoints: Describes parsing raw text into named fields before anything else
Explains normalization into one shared schema so sources can be compared
Shows correlation by a shared key within a time window
Names a real limit, such as parser drift silently producing empty fields or lost evidence

suggested.rationale: That mission practises parsing a log with loops, conditions and dictionaries, which is the core parse-and-normalize skill this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Network logs are records of who talked to whom on a cloud network, without recording what was said. Think of a post office that keeps a ledger of every envelope: sender, receiver, time, and whether it was delivered or turned away, but not the letter inside. In AWS, three log sources cover this. One records conversations between machines inside a network. One records traffic crossing the hub that joins several networks. One records name lookups, the phone-book requests machines make before they connect. Choosing which of these to turn on, and where to keep them, decides whether you can later see an attacker move.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server in your private network starts sending data to an unfamiliar internet address late at night. Before any teaching, list the records you would want to figure out which machine sent the data, where it went, and what name it looked up first. Then say which of those a single kind of network log would not be able to give you.
lessons.teach:
Start with the definitions. A virtual private cloud (VPC) is your own isolated network inside AWS. A subnet is a slice of that network. A network interface is the virtual card one machine uses to connect.
