Optional guardrails are extra rules you switch on for particular OUs, such as restricting which regions may be used. Custom controls are rules you author yourself, built from your own preventive policies or detective rules and attached to an OU in the same way.

Why it works: once an account is placed under an OU, the controls on that OU apply to it without anyone configuring that account by hand. Existing accounts can be enrolled into a registered OU, but they must first meet prerequisites, and conflicting settings they already have must be resolved before enrollment succeeds.

Worked example: a team wants no one in its OU to use a region outside Europe. Step one, enable an optional region-deny guardrail on that OU. Step two, a new account created in that OU inherits it. Step three, an engineer tries to launch a resource in a non-approved region, and the preventive policy rejects the call. Step four, the detective view shows the account as compliant.

Common mistake: treating a detective guardrail as if it stops anything. It only reports; a resource can exist in a non-compliant state until someone remediates it.

Consequence: if a guardrail is enabled on the wrong OU, every account beneath it changes behaviour at once, which can break deployments that depend on the blocked action.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics runs a custom control, which is a rule the company writes itself from a preventive policy (a service control policy, or SCP, that blocks API calls before they happen) and attaches to an organizational unit (OU, a group of accounts managed through AWS Organizations). Its goal is to stop anyone in the OU named Freight-Dev from turning off the shipment-tracking log stream. Step one: author a custom preventive policy that denies the action of disabling that log stream. Step two: [missing]. Step three: a new account created in Freight-Dev inherits the control. Step four: an engineer tries to disable the log stream in that new account, and the call is rejected before it runs. What belongs in the missing step two?
choices: Attach the custom policy to the Freight-Dev OU, the same way any control is attached.
Set the policy's tags so the auditor can find it later.
Enable a detective AWS Config rule in the management account, which will stop the calls.
Delete the existing accounts in Freight-Dev so the control applies cleanly.
questions.why: A custom control is attached to an OU in the same way as a built-in guardrail, and attaching it to Freight-Dev is what makes new accounts in that OU inherit it.

questions.prompt: A platform team at a grocery chain describes one of its controls as recording whether each resource is compliant and reporting drift afterwards, without ever stopping a call. Which kind of guardrail is this?
choices: An optional guardrail, because it can only be switched on for particular OUs.
A custom control, because the team wrote it themselves from a service control policy.
A preventive guardrail, because it blocks API calls before they happen.
A detective guardrail, because it records compliance and reports drift after the fact.
questions.why: Detective guardrails are implemented as AWS Config rules that record compliance and report drift, and they do not block anything; the other options describe preventive or categorical labels that do not match this behaviour.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to enroll an existing account, which already has a conflicting setting on one of its resources, into a registered OU. Enrollment fails. What is the correct next step?
choices: Enroll the account into a different OU that has no guardrails, then move it later.
Meet the enrollment prerequisites and resolve the conflicting settings, then enroll the account.
Delete the account's logging so the conflict disappears, then enroll.
Move the account into the OU anyway and wait for the conflict to clear by itself.
questions.why: Existing accounts must meet prerequisites and have conflicting settings resolved before enrollment succeeds, so fixing those is the required action.

questions.prompt: A retailer has three OUs: Stores-Edge, Stores-Core and Finance. Its platform engineer enables an optional region-restriction guardrail on the root of the organization instead of on Stores-Edge alone. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Only the management account changes behaviour, because it is the one that owns the guardrail.
Every account beneath the root changes behaviour at once, which can break deployments that depend on the blocked region.
Nothing changes until someone manually runs remediation on each account.
Finance is protected automatically, but Stores-Edge is unaffected because it has its own settings.
questions.why: A guardrail applied to a high-level point in the hierarchy takes effect on every account beneath it immediately, so deployments relying on the blocked action can fail across all those accounts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how AWS Control Tower keeps new accounts secure from the start, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on its guardrails, including what happens to an existing account that does not yet meet them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Control Tower gives us a landing zone: accounts sit in organizational units, and guardrails are attached to those units so every new account inherits them the moment it is created. Preventive guardrails use service control policies to stop forbidden actions, and detective guardrails use AWS Config rules to report drift. Optional guardrails let us add rules for specific units, and custom controls let us encode our own policy. The main limit is that detective guardrails only report; a non-compliant resource stays non-compliant until someone fixes it. Bringing an existing account in also means it must meet the prerequisites and resolve conflicting settings first, so some accounts may need cleanup before enrollment. The tradeoff is that a guardrail on a high-level unit affects everything beneath it, so a mistake there spreads widely.
rubricPoints: Explains that accounts in an OU inherit guardrails automatically at creation
Distinguishes preventive guardrails (block the action) from detective guardrails (report drift)
States that detective guardrails do not stop a non-compliant resource by themselves
Names a limit: existing accounts need prerequisites met and conflicts resolved before enrollment, and a broad guardrail affects all accounts beneath it

suggested.rationale: No listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers Control Tower's landing zone, guardrails, or enrollment, so reading the teaching text and checking the console is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Organization policies are rules set at the top of a group of cloud accounts that limit what those accounts can do, no matter what their own administrators have granted. Think of a building manager who says no tenant may bring gas stoves onto any floor, and that rule holds even if one tenant wants one. These rules come in four kinds. Some limit what people and services may do, some limit who may act on a resource, one kind stops AI services from using your content, and one kind fixes configuration settings across services. Knowing which kind does what keeps a brand-new account safe from its first minute.
lessons.guessPrompt: An administrator in a member account has a policy that allows launching servers anywhere. An organization-level rule denies launching servers in one region. Can that administrator launch a server in that region, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A service control policy (SCP) is an organization-level guardrail that sets the maximum permissions that identities in an account or group of accounts can ever use. It grants nothing by itself. A user still needs an identity policy that allows an action, and the action works only where both the guardrail and that grant allow it. A resource control policy (RCP) does a similar job for resources: it caps what can be done to a resource, including requests from callers outside your organization. A declarative policy is different. It sets a desired configuration for a supported service, such as blocking public access to certain settings, and the service enforces that setting across accounts. An AI services opt-out policy stops AWS AI services from using your content to improve their services for the accounts it covers.

Why it works: the guardrail is checked on every request, so it applies even to the most powerful administrator role in a member account. The policy attaches to an organizational unit (a named group of accounts), so any account placed in that unit inherits it the moment it joins.

Worked example: an SCP on the Engineering unit denies launching compute in any region except two approved ones. An engineer with full administrator rights in an Engineering account tries to launch a server in a third region. Step 1: the administrator's identity policy allows the action. Step 2: the SCP denies the action in that region. Step 3: an explicit deny always wins, so the request fails. The same request in an approved region succeeds, because the guardrail allows it there.

Common mistake: assuming an SCP grants access, or that it limits the management account. An SCP cannot give anyone permission, and it does not restrict the management account.

Consequence: a new account placed in a unit with a too-strict guardrail may be unable to do its job from creation, and one placed in a unit with a too-loose guardrail is exposed from creation. Placement decisions are security decisions.

questions.prompt: Harbor Dental keeps patient scans in one S3 bucket and has attached a resource control policy (RCP) to it that allows reads only from principals inside its own AWS organization. A contractor's role in a separate account that is not in the organization has an identity policy that allows s3:GetObject on that bucket. Step 1: the contractor's identity policy allows the read. Step 2: the bucket's RCP is checked for a caller outside the organization, and it does not allow that caller. Step 3: [missing]. What is the outcome?
choices: Because the identity policy allows the read, the request succeeds and the RCP is ignored.
The request is denied only if the contractor's account is the bucket owner, because RCPs restrict owner accounts alone.
The request succeeds only after the contractor's account is added to the organization's SCP allowlist.
The request is denied, because the RCP caps what can be done to the bucket and no part of it allows this outside caller.
questions.why: An RCP sets a ceiling on what can be done to a resource, including from outside callers, so an outside request needs both the identity grant and an RCP that allows it, and here the RCP does not.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a service control policy (SCP) is accurate?
choices: An SCP can be attached to a single user to override the rules of their organizational unit.
An SCP is the place where a user's access is granted, so attaching one to a unit lets its accounts run new actions.
An SCP sets the most that identities in covered accounts can ever do, and a user still needs an identity policy that allows the action.
An SCP applies only to resources such as buckets and queues, not to the identities that call them.
questions.why: An SCP is a maximum-permissions guardrail that grants nothing by itself, so an action works only where both the SCP and an identity policy allow it.

questions.prompt: A Retail organizational unit has an SCP that denies s3:DeleteBucket for every account in the unit. An administrator signed in to the management account, which is not in the Retail unit, deletes a bucket that the management account owns. What happens?
choices: The deletion is blocked, because every account in the organization is subject to the SCP.
The deletion is blocked only if the administrator's identity policy is also missing the action.
The deletion succeeds, because SCPs do not restrict the management account.
The deletion succeeds only if the bucket is empty when the SCP is evaluated.
questions.why: SCPs do not restrict the management account, and this bucket is owned there, so no SCP in the Retail unit applies to the deletion.

questions.prompt: A compliance lead wants AWS AI services to be stopped from using the company's content to improve those services, across every account in the organization, including accounts created next year. Which policy type fits this goal?
choices: A service control policy that denies the AI service API actions.
A declarative policy that sets the AI service's data-use setting.
An AI services opt-out policy attached at the organization level.
A resource control policy attached to each S3 bucket.
questions.why: An AI services opt-out policy is the policy type that stops AWS AI services from using content from the accounts it covers, and attaching it at the organization level covers new accounts too.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an SCP and an RCP, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on an SCP to protect a new account.
lessons.modelAnswer: An SCP sets the most an identity in a member account can do. It never grants anything, so an administrator still needs an identity policy that allows an action, and the action works only where both allow it. An SCP applies to identities in member accounts and does not restrict the management account. An RCP does the same job for resources: it caps what can happen to a resource, including requests from outside the organization. The main tradeoff of an SCP is that it is blunt. If I deny a service broadly to protect a new account, I may also block a legitimate workload, and the guardrail applies to everyone in that unit, including roles that were meant to do the blocked task. So I would test a change in a sandbox unit first and handle exceptions through a separate unit rather than weakening the shared rule.
rubricPoints: SCPs cap the permissions of identities in member accounts and never grant access on their own.
RCPs cap what can be done to resources, including requests from outside the organization.
Effective access is the overlap between the guardrail and the identity or resource policy.
A broad guardrail can block legitimate work, so changes need testing and scoped exceptions.

suggested.rationale: The authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace allow and deny outcomes across guardrail layers, which is the reasoning this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Security services such as threat detection and compliance checking need to look across every account in a company. Rather than logging into each account to switch them on, an organization picks one trusted member account as the delegated administrator for each service. That account can then view and set the service's configuration for all member accounts. The management account, which created the organization, keeps control of who receives that delegation. Think of a building owner who appoints a security chief for the alarm system. The chief can manage every floor's alarms from one panel, but cannot hand out master keys or rebuild the building.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has ten cloud accounts and wants one threat-detection service to watch all of them. Would you switch it on in each account by hand, or set it up once from a central place? What would you worry about with each choice?
lessons.teach:
A management account is the single account that creates an AWS Organization and is the only place that can grant delegated administrator status. A member account is any other account inside that organization. A delegated administrator is a member account that a specific service trusts to manage that service's settings and findings for every member account. Before delegation works, the service must have trusted access enabled in the organization, which lets it act across accounts. The idea works because the management account hands out a bounded role. Security staff can then work from a dedicated security account and keep the management account free of everyday workloads.

Worked example: account M is the management account, account S is the security account, and accounts A and B are members. Step 1: from M, enable trusted access for the threat-detection service. Step 2: from M, register S as the delegated administrator for that service. Step 3: from S, turn the service on with automatic enrollment, so any new account C joins it the moment it is created. Step 4: findings from A, B and C all appear in S, and S can change the settings for all three without logging into any of them.

Common mistake: assuming the delegated administrator can change the organization itself. It cannot create accounts, restructure the organization, or nominate another delegate. Those powers stay with the management account.

Consequence: because S holds organization-wide visibility and control, an attacker who compromises S can weaken security across every member account. S therefore needs strict access controls, its own logging, and no everyday workloads.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has a management account 1111 and a security account 2222. It wants an exposure-scanning service, which looks for publicly open storage buckets, to cover every member account, including accounts created later. The team's plan has three steps. Step 1: [missing]. Step 2: from account 1111, register account 2222 as the delegated administrator for the scanner. Step 3: from account 2222, turn on the scanner with automatic enrollment. Which action fills the missing step 1?
choices: From account 1111, enable trusted access for the exposure-scanning service across the organization.
From account 1111, log into each existing account and switch the scanner on.
From account 1111, create a new member account for the data team.
From account 2222, register itself as the delegated administrator so it can enroll new accounts.
questions.why: Trusted access must be enabled from the management account before any delegation can happen, so enabling it across the organization is the missing first step.

questions.prompt: A company runs an organization with member accounts 4410, 4411 and 4412. Which account is the only one that can grant delegated administrator status for a security service?
choices: Account 4411, the member account that holds the company's central log archive.
Any member account that has been given full administrator permissions.
The management account, the account that created the organization.
The first account that switched the security service on in the console.
questions.why: Only the management account can grant delegated administrator status, because that power sits with the account that created the organization.

questions.prompt: Delegated administrator account 7720 for a threat-detection service is asked to create a new member account for a contractor and to nominate a second delegate for the same service. What is the correct outcome?
choices: It can nominate the second delegate, but creating accounts is reserved for the management account alone.
It can do both, because being trusted for the service gives it full control of the organization.
It can create the account only if trusted access has been turned off first.
It cannot do either, because creating accounts and nominating delegates stay with the management account.
questions.why: A delegated administrator manages the service's settings and findings, but cannot create accounts, restructure the organization or nominate another delegate, so both requests must go to the management account.

questions.prompt: Account 9056 is the delegated administrator for a compliance-checking service in an organization with 40 member accounts. An attacker gains console access to account 9056. Which response best reflects the risk?
choices: Nothing changes, since each member keeps its own separate settings and the delegate has no reach into them at all.
The attacker could weaken security settings across all 40 members, so the account needs strict access controls, its own logging and no everyday workloads.
The attacker sees findings only for account 9056 itself, so the blast radius stays within that single account and no new controls are needed.
The attacker can delete the organization and every member account, because delegated administrators hold that power directly.
questions.why: Because the delegate holds organization-wide visibility and control over the service, a compromise there can weaken protections in every member account, which is why it needs tight access control, its own logging and no everyday workloads.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we don't just run our security tools from the management account. Explain delegated administrator accounts to them in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of delegating.
lessons.modelAnswer: The management account creates the organization and controls who holds which powers, so it should stay small and locked down. Running security tools there would mix routine security work with the most powerful account in the organization. A delegated administrator is a member account, usually a dedicated security account, that a specific service trusts to manage that service's settings and findings across all member accounts. The management account grants this per service, so the security team can work from a separate account. The tradeoff is concentration of risk: the delegated account now sees and can change security settings for the whole organization, so if it is compromised, the impact spreads widely. That is why it needs tight access control and its own audit logging. Delegation also doesn't let that account restructure the organization or assign another delegate.
rubricPoints: Explains that the management account keeps the organization's top powers and should be kept minimal.
Defines a delegated administrator as a member account given org-wide authority over one specific service.
Names the tradeoff that compromising the delegated account has organization-wide impact.
States that the delegate cannot change the organization structure or appoint other delegates.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about who holds which powers and why, which a learner shows best by explaining it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Every AWS account is created with one all-powerful sign-in called the root user. It can do anything in the account, including things no other login can do, and permission rules you write cannot take those powers away. Managing it means deciding who holds that sign-in, protecting it with strong sign-in checks, removing copies that are not needed, and having a planned emergency route for the rare time a person must use it. For a company with many accounts, the goal is to avoid a separate, unguarded root sign-in sitting in each one.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company has fifty accounts, each with its own root sign-in and a password kept in a shared spreadsheet, what is the biggest risk you would worry about first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. The root user is the sign-in identity created with every account, and it has unrestricted power in that account. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means signing in requires a second proof beyond a password, such as a code from a device or a hardware key. A member account is an account that belongs to an organization and is governed from a central management account. Break-glass access is a pre-planned emergency way to get powerful access when normal routes fail. It is deliberately hard to use and watched closely.

Why it works. Because ordinary permission rules cannot limit the root user, protection has to come from outside those rules: strong MFA on the sign-in, no long-lived root access keys, and removing root credentials from member accounts where they are not needed. Centralized root access lets the management account hold that control. Member accounts can have their root credentials removed, and the few tasks that truly need root are performed through short-lived, tightly scoped root sessions started from the management account and logged.

Worked example. A member account was created last year, and its root sign-in still has a password and an MFA device belonging to a former employee. Step 1: list who can sign in as root. Step 2: confirm the account has no root access keys. Step 3: check whether daily work runs through roles, which would mean root credentials can be removed. Step 4: if a task truly needs root, such as changing an account-level setting, use a centrally governed root session and record who did it and why. Step 5: write the break-glass steps and test that the sealed emergency credentials still work.

Common mistake. Teams treat root MFA as a box to tick and bind it to one person's personal phone. When that person leaves, nobody can recover the account.

Consequence. A root sign-in with stolen credentials can change billing, close the account, or disable the security tools that would have caught it, so any unexpected root sign-in should trigger an immediate alert.

Root protection is a control you design around the account, not a permission you can narrow.

questions.prompt: A payments firm runs a member account called ledger-eu. Its team has done the following: (1) found that the root sign-in's MFA device is a phone registered to an engineer who left last spring; (2) confirmed the account has no root access keys; (3) confirmed that all deployment work runs through roles, not root. Next they need to change the account's tax contact, which is an account-level setting that only root can change. Their steps then jump to (5) record the outcome in the audit log. The missing step between 3 and 5 is the one that performs the tax contact change. Which step fills that gap?
choices: Start a short-lived root session from the management account, make the tax contact change, and log who did it and why.
Create a new root access key in the member account so the change can be scripted.
Email the departed engineer's phone number to re-enroll the MFA device before doing anything else.
Delete the ledger-eu account and recreate it so the tax contact can be set from scratch.
questions.why: The teaching text says tasks that truly need root should use a short-lived, tightly scoped root session started from the management account and logged, rather than long-lived keys or re-enrolling a personal device.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a break-glass procedure for its member accounts. Which description best fits what break-glass access is meant to be?
choices: A pre-planned emergency route to powerful access when normal routes fail, deliberately hard to use and watched closely.
A permission rule that gives read-only access to billing data during normal business hours.
A second sign-in for the root user that is shared openly across the team chat channel.
A standing admin role that every senior engineer uses daily so no one waits for approval.
questions.why: The teaching text defines break-glass access as a pre-planned emergency path to powerful access that is deliberately hard to use and watched closely, which is the only choice matching that definition.

questions.prompt: A retail company set root MFA on one buyer's personal phone in a member account with 12 other engineers on the team. The buyer leaves the company and the phone is wiped. What is the most accurate description of what went wrong?
choices: The root user's password was too short, so anyone could guess it after the phone was wiped.
The engineers' role permissions were too broad, which blocked the root sign-in from completing.
The account automatically deleted itself because a member account cannot have MFA on a personal device.
The MFA was tied to one person rather than a recoverable, team-wide arrangement, so nobody could complete a root sign-in.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that binding root MFA to one person's personal phone means that when the person leaves, nobody can recover the account, so the failure is the single-person dependency.

questions.prompt: A healthcare provider's security team sees a root sign-in to one member account at 3 a.m. that nobody on the team expected. What is the response the teaching text recommends?
choices: Assume it is harmless because root can only read logs and cannot make changes.
Wait for the next weekly review to see whether the sign-in happens again.
Trigger an immediate alert, because a root sign-in with stolen credentials can change billing, close the account, or disable security tools.
Rotate the root user's password only, since the MFA device cannot be compromised.
questions.why: The teaching text says any unexpected root sign-in should trigger an immediate alert because root can change billing, close the account, or disable security tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up root access for a new member account, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach, such as emergency access being slower.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by removing root credentials from the new member account if the team can do its daily work through roles, so nobody has a standing root password or access keys there. Anything that truly needs root, such as an account-level setting, would go through a short-lived root session started from the management account, which is logged and tied to a reason. For the root sign-in that must remain for emergencies, I would enable strong MFA using a hardware key or passkey held by more than one trusted person, not a personal phone. I would also write a break-glass procedure: sealed credentials, a named approver, an alert on any root sign-in, and a review afterward. The tradeoff is that genuine emergencies become slower, because someone has to go through the approval and session steps instead of signing in directly. I accept that delay because it leaves a clear record and far fewer ways for a stolen root login to do damage.
rubricPoints: Explains that root credentials in member accounts should be removed or avoided where roles can do the work
Describes task-scoped, logged root sessions from the management account for the few tasks that need root
Covers strong MFA held by more than one trusted person, not a single personal device
Names a break-glass procedure with alerting and review, and states a tradeoff such as slower emergency access

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers root credentials, so explaining the break-glass tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing your cloud resources, such as networks, storage buckets and permissions, in a text file rather than clicking them together by hand. That file is a template. Deploying it creates a stack, a named group of resources that can be updated or deleted as one unit. Because the description is text, you can review it, test it, and check it against security rules before anything is built. This objective covers four ways to make that repeatable and safe: a tool that deploys one template across many accounts, a syntax checker, a policy checker, and other vendors' tools that do similar jobs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team runs ten cloud accounts and writes one template that creates a storage bucket. Before any tool is involved, what different kinds of mistake could that template contain, and which of those mistakes would a syntax checker be unable to catch?
lessons.teach:
A template is a file that describes the resources you want. A stack is one deployed copy of a template, tracked as a unit. A StackSet is a CloudFormation feature that deploys one template as a stack into many target accounts and regions, driven from a central administrator account, so the same baseline lands everywhere. Policy as code means writing security rules in a machine-readable form so a program can check them automatically.

cfn-lint is a syntax and schema checker. It reads a template and reports errors such as misspelled property names, values that a resource type does not allow, or references to things that do not exist. It catches mistakes before deployment, but it does not judge whether a choice is secure.

CloudFormation Guard is a policy-as-code tool. You write rules in its own small language, for example that every storage bucket must block public access, and it evaluates templates against those rules. A failing rule becomes a finding that can stop the build. Third-party IaC tools such as Terraform or Pulumi work on the same principle with their own languages and plugins, so the idea transfers even when the product changes.

Worked example: a template creates a bucket with public access left on. cfn-lint passes because the syntax is valid. Guard fails the rule requiring public access to be blocked. The pipeline stops, the template is corrected, and only then is the StackSet rolled out to forty accounts.

Common mistake: treating a passing linter as proof of security. Syntax validity and policy compliance are different checks, and a secure pipeline needs both.

Consequence: a flawed template in a StackSet is copied into every target account at once, so one review gap becomes forty exposures.

questions.prompt: A payments company has a template that creates a message queue for transaction events, with server-side encryption (scrambling stored data so it is unreadable without a key) turned off. The company deploys the template as a StackSet to 12 accounts. Step 1: the syntax checker cfn-lint runs and reports no errors, because the property names and values are valid. Step 2: CloudFormation Guard runs a rule requiring every queue to have encryption enabled, and it reports a failing finding. Step 3: the pipeline halts and an engineer enables encryption in the template. Step 4: the step that is still missing before the StackSet can safely go out is the one shown in the choices.
choices: Re-run both cfn-lint and Guard against the corrected template, confirm it passes, and then roll out the StackSet.
Turn off the Guard rule for this template, because a failing rule is only a warning and does not stop the build.
Deploy the StackSet to the 12 accounts now, since cfn-lint already passed on the original template.
Delete the queue in every account so the template can be applied again from a clean state.
questions.why: The corrected template has to pass both the syntax check and the policy check again before the StackSet is rolled out, because a passing syntax check alone does not show policy compliance.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what cfn-lint, the syntax and schema checker for CloudFormation templates, is designed to find?
choices: Resources that are reachable from the public internet, because it scans network settings.
Whether the IAM roles in the template follow least privilege, because it reads the permission documents.
Stored data that is unencrypted, because it inspects every storage resource for encryption settings.
Misspelled property names, values a resource type does not allow, and references to things that do not exist.
questions.why: cfn-lint checks syntax and schema validity, such as bad property names, disallowed values and broken references, and it does not judge whether a configuration is secure.

questions.prompt: A security team rolls out one template as a StackSet to 25 accounts across three regions. The template opens a database port to all internet addresses. Nothing in the pipeline caught it before rollout. What is the most accurate description of the resulting exposure?
choices: The exposure is limited to the first region the StackSet deploys to, and the other regions are protected by default.
Nothing is exposed until someone manually copies the template to each account, since StackSets only create empty stacks.
The same open port is created in every targeted account and region at once, so the single review gap becomes many exposures.
Only the administrator account is exposed, because StackSet changes are applied centrally and then reviewed.
questions.why: A StackSet copies one template into every target account and region, so a single flaw is replicated everywhere at once.

questions.prompt: A platform lead argues that because every infrastructure template in the pipeline passes cfn-lint, the team does not need a policy-as-code tool like CloudFormation Guard. Which response best identifies the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: cfn-lint is only allowed to run on templates with fewer than 100 resources, so its results are unreliable at scale.
Passing cfn-lint shows the template is syntactically valid, but a valid template can still be insecure, so policy rules must be checked separately.
cfn-lint and Guard perform the same check, so running both is redundant and wastes build time.
Policy rules can only be written in the template itself, so a separate tool is never needed for them.
questions.why: Syntax validity and policy compliance are different checks, so a clean cfn-lint result does not prove that a template meets the security rules a Guard rule would enforce.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a pipeline should run both a syntax checker and a policy checker before a StackSet deploys a template to every account, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on policy checks alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: The syntax checker, cfn-lint, asks whether the template is valid: are the property names real, are the values allowed for that resource type, and do references point to things that exist. That protects us from deployments that fail halfway. It says nothing about whether the bucket is safe. The policy checker, Guard, asks whether the template follows our rules, such as no public buckets. Both are needed because a template can be perfectly valid and still insecure. The main tradeoff with policy checks is coverage: a rule only catches what someone thought to write, so a risk nobody encoded passes silently. Also, a StackSet multiplies whatever gets through, so the gate has to sit before the rollout, not after it.
rubricPoints: Syntax validation and policy compliance check different things
A valid template can still be insecure
Policy rules only catch risks someone has encoded as a rule
The checks must run before a StackSet rollout because the template is copied to every target account

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about why two different checks are needed and where each one stops, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A tag is a small label you attach to a cloud resource, such as a server, a database or a storage bucket. Each label is a pair: a key, like department, and a value, like payments. Once resources carry the same labels, you can filter, sort and total them by those labels. Teams use this to answer everyday questions: which department runs this, which budget pays for it, and is it a production system or a test copy. Tags do not change how a resource behaves. They only describe it, so their value depends on applying them consistently.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs 300 servers across five teams. The finance team asks how much the payments team spent last month. What information would you need attached to each server to answer that without checking every server by hand?
lessons.teach:
A tag is a key-value pair attached to a resource. The key names a category, such as department, cost-center or environment, and the value fills it in, such as payments, CC-4410 or prod. The cloud provider stores tags as metadata next to the resource, so tags do not change what the resource does. Reports, resource lists and access rules can then group or filter by those pairs. In AWS, tags are the standard way to do this across services.

Why it works: a report is really a query over labels. If every resource carries the same key spelled the same way, one filter returns the whole group. Cost reporting is the most common use. Spend is totalled per tag value, so a cost-center tag becomes the key for splitting a bill. Tags can also feed access rules, letting a policy allow a team to stop only the resources whose department tag matches its own.

Worked example. An instance is tagged department=payments, environment=prod and cost-center=CC-4410. Step 1: the cost report is set to group by the cost-center tag. Step 2: the report finds this instance and adds its compute spend to the CC-4410 row. Step 3: a second instance tagged department=payments, environment=test, cost-center=CC-4410 also lands in that row. Step 4: an instance with no cost-center tag lands in an untagged group that nobody owns.

Common mistake: inconsistent keys or values. Writing Department on one server and department on another, or Prod in one place and production in another, splits one group into several. Keys and values are usually case-sensitive, so the grouping fails silently.

Consequence: in a running system, untagged or mis-tagged resources become spend nobody can explain. An access rule keyed to a tag simply will not match them, so the wrong team may get access or the right team may be locked out. Cost allocation tags must also be activated in billing before they appear in cost reports, and they usually apply only from that point forward.

Tags describe resources; consistent, enforced tagging is what makes the groups trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company tags a new fleet of batch servers with project=relay on 3 March. Its finance lead activates the project tag in billing settings on 10 March, then opens the March cost report grouped by project. Trace it. Step 1: the servers carry project=relay from 3 March. Step 2: the tag is activated in billing on 10 March. Step 3: the March report is grouped by the project tag, and the relay row shows the servers' spend from 10 March onward. Step 4: the spend from 3 to 9 March, before activation, is ____. Which phrase completes step 4?
choices: is not split by the project tag, so it does not appear in the relay row
is deleted from the bill, because inactive tags are removed from reports
moves into the relay row, because tags apply retroactively to all past usage
creates a relay row showing zero spend until the next billing cycle
questions.why: Cost allocation tags must be activated before they appear in cost reports and usually apply only from activation forward, so the earlier spend is not grouped under relay.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union wants to know what a tag is. Which description fits best?
choices: A key-value pair stored as metadata beside a resource that groups or filters it without changing what the resource does
A password that limits who can open a resource
A billing invoice line that is created each time a resource starts
A separate copy of a resource kept for backup purposes
questions.why: The teaching text defines a tag as a key-value pair stored as metadata next to the resource, used for grouping and filtering, and says tags do not change what the resource does.

questions.prompt: A retail company has an access rule that lets its dev team stop any instance whose environment tag equals dev. One instance is tagged Environment=Dev. What is the most likely result?
choices: The rule matches the instance because the tag key and value mean the same thing to people
The rule does not match, so the instance is not covered and the team may be locked out of it
The rule matches only after the tag is activated in billing
The rule matches but the team sees a warning in the cost report
questions.why: Keys and values are usually case-sensitive, so Environment and Dev do not match environment and dev, and an access rule keyed to the tag will not apply to that instance.

questions.prompt: A cost report is grouped by the cost-center tag. Four resources exist: a web tier tagged CC-220 with 300 dollars of spend, a batch job tagged CC-220 with 150 dollars, a log store with no cost-center tag and 80 dollars, and a reporting instance tagged CC-305 with 200 dollars. What total appears in the CC-220 row?
choices: 730 dollars
530 dollars
300 dollars
450 dollars
questions.why: The CC-220 row totals the spend of resources whose cost-center value is CC-220, which is 300 plus 150, giving 450 dollars; the untagged log store and the CC-305 instance are excluded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we tag resources with department, cost center and environment, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on tags.
lessons.modelAnswer: Tags are key-value labels on each resource. We use three keys because they answer three different questions: department says who owns the resource, cost center says which budget pays for it, and environment says whether it is production, test or development. Reports and access rules can then group by those labels without anyone checking each server. The main limit is that tags are only as good as their consistency and coverage. A typo such as Prod versus production splits a group, and an untagged resource falls into no group at all. Tags also describe rather than enforce, so someone can still create a resource without them unless we add a check that blocks or flags it. Cost allocation tags need to be switched on in billing before they show in cost reports, and they usually apply only from that point forward, so historical spend may stay unassigned.
rubricPoints: A tag is a key-value label on a resource that describes it without changing how it behaves.
Department, cost center and environment answer ownership, budget and risk questions respectively.
Tags work only when keys and values are spelled and cased consistently and applied to every resource.
Cost allocation tags must be activated in billing and usually apply only from that point forward.
Tags describe resources, so they need enforcement such as required-tag checks to be trustworthy.

suggested.rationale: Attributing spend to tag values is the core skill, and the planned cost model engine would let the learner group fictional spend by cost-center and environment tags.

lessons.plain: Imagine a building manager who sets the locks, cameras and alarm rules once for every office in a company, rather than walking into each office to set them by hand. AWS Firewall Manager applies that idea to cloud accounts. A central administrator defines a security rule set and says which accounts and resources it covers. The service then pushes the rules out and reports which resources do not match them. It works across an organization of many accounts, so a new account picks up the baseline without someone remembering to configure it. Firewall here means a set of network and web filtering controls, not a single device.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your company has 40 AWS accounts and a new web filtering rule must be on every public web endpoint. Would you rather edit each account by hand, or have one place that applies the rule everywhere and flags any endpoint missing it? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Firewall Manager is a central service for defining security policies once and applying them across many accounts in an AWS Organization. An organization is the grouping of accounts that a company manages together, and each of those accounts is a member account. Firewall Manager is run from a delegated administrator account, which is a member account given the job of managing security tooling for the whole organization, so the main management account does not have to do it.

A policy in this service names the type of control it enforces, such as a web application firewall rule set, shield protection for internet-facing resources, a set of security groups every workload must carry, or a network firewall configuration. It also names the scope, meaning which accounts, organizational units (named groups of accounts) and resource tags it covers. Finally it says whether non-compliant resources should be corrected automatically or only reported.

Why it works: the policy lives in one place, and the service keeps checking covered resources. A resource created later in a covered account is evaluated without anyone running a script. Compliance results roll up per policy and per account, which is the evidence a reviewer asks for.

Worked example: a policy requires a particular web application firewall on every public load balancer. Step 1: the administrator creates the policy and scopes it to the Production organizational unit. Step 2: a team launches a new load balancer in a Production account. Step 3: the service detects the resource, finds no firewall attached, and marks it non-compliant. Step 4: depending on the policy settings, it either attaches the firewall or raises a finding for someone to fix.

Common mistake: assuming the service sees resources it has not been told about. The scope and the recorded resource configuration determine what gets checked. A resource type that is not recorded, or an account outside the scope, produces no result, which looks like compliance when it is really a blind spot.

Consequence: a missed scope means an internet-facing endpoint can run unprotected while the central dashboard still looks clean.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs its Firewall Manager policies from a delegated administrator account, which is a member account given the job of managing security tooling for the whole organization. The security team writes a policy that requires a network firewall configuration on every resource tagged data-class=regulated, and sets the policy to report only, not to correct automatically. Step 1: the administrator creates the policy with that tag as its scope. Step 2: an engineer creates a virtual network in member account 4471 and tags it data-class=regulated. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the compliance results for account 4471 show that the policy has found a non-compliant resource, and a finding is raised for someone to fix.
choices: The service attaches the network firewall configuration immediately, because the policy scope always overrides the correction setting.
The service skips the check because tags apply only to accounts and never to individual resources.
The service evaluates the virtual network against the required firewall configuration, finds none attached, and marks it non-compliant without changing it, since correction is set to report only.
The service ignores the virtual network because a different team created it from the team that wrote the policy.
questions.why: The service checks each covered resource against the policy, and with automatic correction turned off it records the non-compliance and reports it rather than fixing the resource.

questions.prompt: In AWS Firewall Manager, what is the purpose of a delegated administrator account?
choices: It is the root user of the main management account, used to approve every policy before it takes effect.
It is the account where every member account's resources are physically stored.
It is a member account that performs the job of managing security tooling for the organization, so the main management account does not have to.
It is a separate organization created only to hold compliance reports for auditors.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the delegated administrator as a member account given the job of managing security tooling for the whole organization, so the main management account is not needed for that work.

questions.prompt: A security engineer scopes a Firewall Manager policy to the Production organizational unit. A team launches a public load balancer in a staging account that is not part of that unit. What does the central dashboard show for that load balancer?
choices: It shows nothing for that account under this policy, which looks like compliance but is actually a blind spot.
It shows an error that stops the policy from running for any account in the organization.
It shows the load balancer as non-compliant, because every public resource in the organization is checked by default.
It shows the load balancer as compliant, because the policy checked it and found a firewall attached.
questions.why: An account outside the scope produces no result, so the dashboard looks clean while the load balancer is not being checked at all.

questions.prompt: A policy is set to report only, and it covers a new public load balancer that has no web application firewall attached. Which outcome matches the teaching text?
choices: The service attaches the firewall automatically within the same evaluation.
The service deletes the load balancer because it does not meet the policy.
The service marks the load balancer as compliant, since reporting only means it does not evaluate resources.
The service marks the load balancer as non-compliant and raises a finding for someone to fix, without attaching anything.
questions.why: When the policy only reports, the service records the non-compliance and raises a finding for a person to act on rather than correcting the resource itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AWS Firewall Manager does for a multi-account organization, and name one limit or tradeoff of managing security this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Firewall Manager lets one administrator, a delegated admin account inside the organization, define a security policy once and apply it to a chosen set of accounts and resources, selected by organizational unit or tags. It keeps evaluating covered resources, so a newly created load balancer or security group in scope is checked without manual setup, and it gives a compliance view per policy and per account. The main tradeoff is blast radius: a mistaken policy change or an overly broad scope can affect many accounts at once, so changes need review and staged rollout. A second limit is visibility. The service only judges what is in scope and what the underlying configuration data records. A resource in an excluded account, or of a type the policy does not cover, is outside its view and still needs other checks. It enforces network and web filtering controls. It does not replace identity controls or sound account structure.
rubricPoints: Describes central policy definition by a delegated administrator for an organization
Explains that scope (accounts, organizational units, tags) determines which resources are covered
Notes continuous evaluation of new resources and per-account compliance reporting
Names a limit or tradeoff such as blast radius of broad scope or blind spots outside scope or recorded data

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers central firewall policy administration, so this is best learned from the product's concepts and console steps.

lessons.plain: Large organizations often run many separate AWS accounts, usually one per team or environment. Sometimes one account holds something the others need, such as a network, a set of approved building blocks, or a shared setting. This lesson covers two safe ways to share that. One way shares a live resource so other accounts can use the original without a copy. The other publishes a curated menu of pre-approved templates that people can launch themselves, within limits the owner sets. The aim is to let teams reuse good things without handing out the keys to everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has ten AWS accounts, and a shared private network subnet lives in one of them. Should you copy that subnet into each account, or let the other accounts use the original? Why?
lessons.teach:
Some terms first. An AWS account is a separate container for resources, with its own permissions and its own bill. A resource is anything you create inside an account, such as a subnet, a database, or a template. Sharing means letting principals (users, roles, or accounts) in another account, or in an organizational unit (a group of accounts), use a resource without owning a copy.

AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) shares supported resource types directly. The owner creates a resource share, names the resources and the recipients, and recipients then use the original. The resource stays in the owner's account, so the owner keeps control. If the owner changes or deletes it, every consumer is affected.

AWS Service Catalog shares curated provisioning. A product is a template for infrastructure, and a portfolio is a collection of products. The owner shares the portfolio with recipient accounts, and their users launch products from it. A launch constraint names an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when it creates resources, so end users need permission to launch the product, not permission to create the underlying resources directly. Other constraints limit which parameter values users may choose.

Worked example. A platform team owns a subnet in a hub account. First, they create a RAM resource share containing that subnet and add the application account as a recipient. The application account can now place instances in it. Second, the team wants a standard database stack. They put its template into a Service Catalog product, add the product to a portfolio, attach a launch constraint role, and share the portfolio with the application account. A developer launches the database without any rights to create databases directly.

Common mistake: assuming that sharing transfers ownership, or that copying a template once is equivalent to sharing it. Copies drift apart over time, while a shared original stays in one place.

Consequence in a running system: deleting or editing a shared subnet or product takes effect for every consumer at once, so changes to shared resources need a review path.

questions.prompt: A finance team in a shared-services account owns a template for an encrypted reporting bucket. They want analysts in reporting account 5582 to create that bucket without being granted rights to create buckets directly. The steps so far: (1) Put the bucket template into a Service Catalog product. (2) [step missing]. (3) Share the portfolio with account 5582. Analysts then launch the product. Which choice correctly fills step 2?
choices: Add the product to a portfolio and attach a launch constraint naming a role that Service Catalog assumes when it creates the bucket.
Give the analysts an IAM policy that allows them to create S3 buckets, so launches succeed.
Create a RAM resource share that contains the bucket template so account 5582 can use it.
Copy the template into account 5582 so the reporting team owns a local version it can edit.
questions.why: Service Catalog products reach consumers through a portfolio, and the launch constraint role lets Service Catalog create the resources so analysts need only launch rights, not direct creation rights.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's network team owns a private subnet in one account and wants six partner accounts to place their workloads in it. The team wants to keep ownership and control of the subnet and avoid maintaining copies. Which approach fits, and why?
choices: Transfer ownership of the subnet to the partner accounts, so each one controls its own version.
Create a Service Catalog product for the subnet and add it to one portfolio, because portfolios are the only way to share network resources.
Export the subnet's settings into a template and have each partner account build its own identical subnet.
Share the subnet with a AWS Resource Access Manager resource share, because the subnet stays in the owner's account and recipients use the original.
questions.why: A resource share keeps the resource in the owner's account while recipients use it, which matches the team's need for control without copies.

questions.prompt: A security engineer deletes a shared media-transcoding subnet from the owning account to clean up old infrastructure. Several consumer accounts were using that subnet at the time. What is the most accurate description of the result?
choices: Nothing changes for the consumers, because each one already holds its own copy of the subnet.
Only the owner's account is affected, because consumers never actually used the owner's resource.
Every consumer is affected at once, because they use the original resource rather than a copy.
Ownership of the subnet moves automatically to the consumer account with the most activity.
questions.why: Shared resources stay in the owner's account, so deleting or changing one takes effect for all consumers at the same time, which is why changes need a review path.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks how a contractor can launch an approved load balancer stack in account 8815 without the contractor having any rights to create load balancers or other networking resources directly. Which mechanism answers this?
choices: Add the contractor's user to the account's administrator group, then restrict the stack parameters by hand.
Publish the stack as a Service Catalog product in a portfolio shared with the contractor, using a launch constraint role so Service Catalog creates the resources.
Give the contractor a copy of the stack template so they can run it in their own account under their own permissions.
Share the owner's load balancer with the contractor through a resource share so they can attach to it.
questions.why: A Service Catalog product with a launch constraint lets the contractor launch the approved stack while Service Catalog, not the contractor, holds the rights to create the underlying resources.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we don't just copy a shared network into every account. Explain in your own words when you would use RAM and when you would use Service Catalog, and name one limit or tradeoff of sharing a live resource.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use RAM when other accounts need a live resource to use as-is, like a subnet. The original stays with the owning account, so there is one source of truth, no drift between copies, and recipients can't alter it. The tradeoff is coupling: if the owner changes or deletes the resource, every consumer feels it, so the owner has to manage who can see it and what happens when it changes. Service Catalog fits when the goal is letting teams launch approved infrastructure themselves. The owner publishes products in a portfolio and attaches a launch constraint role, so users get the result without broad permissions. Its limit is that it governs provisioning, not ongoing ownership. Once a product is launched, the resulting stack belongs to the launching account, so later upgrades and drift need separate handling.
rubricPoints: RAM shares a live resource so consumers use the original without copies
Shared resources stay owned by the sharing account, so changes affect all consumers
Service Catalog publishes approved products in portfolios that other accounts can launch
A launch constraint role lets users provision without broad direct permissions
Sharing a live resource couples consumers to the owner's changes and deletions
Launched products belong to the launching account, so drift and upgrades need separate handling

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises cross-account sharing, so reading the concepts and console flow is the best fit for now.

lessons.plain: When a cloud account holds many resources, some drift away from the rules the organization set, such as a storage bucket left open to the public or a disk that is not encrypted. This objective is about AWS services that work together to spot those cases and respond. One service records how each resource is configured over time and checks it against rules. Another gathers the resulting findings in one place and scores them against security standards. A third piece sends a message to a person or channel when something needs attention. Think of a building inspector who keeps a file on every room, marks the rooms that break code, and phones the site manager when a serious problem appears.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a developer creates a storage bucket that anyone on the internet can read, and nobody notices for a week. What would you want in place so the problem is flagged automatically, and who should hear about it first?
lessons.teach:
A resource is any single thing in your cloud account, such as a storage bucket, a virtual server or a database. Its configuration is the set of settings that describe it. A compliance rule is a check that says what a correct configuration must look like, for example that a bucket must block public access. AWS Config is the service that records configurations and evaluates them. It keeps a configuration item, a snapshot of a resource's settings each time they change, so you have a history. It evaluates each resource against config rules, either managed rules supplied by AWS or custom rules you write, and labels the resource compliant or noncompliant. It can also attach a remediation, which is an automated fix that runs a stored runbook (a Systems Manager Automation document) to correct the setting.

AWS Security Hub sits above that. It collects findings from Config, from threat detection and from other security tools, converts them into one common format, removes duplicates, and scores them against standards. A finding is one reported problem with a severity level.

Notifications come from the event bus. Config and Security Hub publish change events, and a routing rule in EventBridge can send matching events to an SNS topic, which emails or pages an operator.

Worked example: someone turns off the public-access block on a bucket. First, Config records a new configuration item. Second, the managed rule for public buckets evaluates it and marks it noncompliant. Third, Security Hub receives that as a failed control with high severity. Fourth, an EventBridge rule matches the high-severity finding and publishes to an SNS topic that alerts the on-call team. Fifth, the attached runbook re-enables the block, and Config evaluates again and marks the bucket compliant.

Common mistake: treating a notification as proof the problem is closed. The resource stays noncompliant until a later evaluation says otherwise, and a failed remediation can retry and then stop without much noise unless you watch for it.

Consequence: an automatic fix can break a live service if it changes a setting the application depends on, so production remediations should be scoped and tested first. Keeping the configuration history is what lets you later answer what a setting was on a given date.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a custom Config rule that flags any load balancer whose security group accepts traffic on port 23 from anywhere. A developer opens port 23 on one load balancer, and the team follows these steps. Step 1: AWS Config records a new configuration item for that load balancer. Step 2: the custom rule evaluates it and marks it noncompliant. Step 3: Security Hub receives the failure as a finding with medium severity. Step 4: ??? Step 5: after the security group is corrected, Config evaluates again and marks the load balancer compliant. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Config deletes the old configuration item to save storage space.
An EventBridge rule matching the medium-severity finding publishes to an SNS topic that emails the network team.
Security Hub marks the load balancer compliant before anyone changes the security group.
The attached runbook runs silently and no operator is told about the finding.
questions.why: Step 4 is the routing step: an EventBridge rule matches the finding and publishes to an SNS topic that notifies a person, which is how notifications reach operators in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: An S3 bucket's public-access setting was changed on 3 March. On 20 March an auditor asks what that setting was on 10 March. Which AWS Config feature lets you answer this?
choices: The configuration history made of configuration items, one snapshot each time settings change
The severity score Security Hub shows on the bucket today
The current match pattern of the EventBridge routing rule
SNS delivery receipts for the alert emails sent in March
questions.why: Config keeps a configuration item each time a resource's settings change, so the history can show what a setting was on a past date.

questions.prompt: A team receives a Security Hub finding for a database that is noncompliant. They see an alert email saying the auto-fix ran, so they close the ticket. Which statement describes the mistake?
choices: Security Hub deletes the finding as soon as the email is sent, so the ticket is unnecessary.
The resource stays noncompliant until a later evaluation marks it compliant, so the ticket should stay open until then.
An alert email proves the database is fixed, so closing the ticket is correct.
Config fixes resources on its own, so no evaluation is ever needed after a runbook runs.
questions.why: A notification only reports that something happened; the resource remains noncompliant until Config evaluates it again and marks it compliant, and a failed remediation can stop quietly.

questions.prompt: A security lead asks which service takes findings from several tools, converts them into one common format, removes duplicates and scores them against standards. Which service is that?
choices: Amazon SNS
AWS Security Hub
AWS Systems Manager
Amazon EventBridge
questions.why: Security Hub is the layer above Config and other tools that normalises, deduplicates and scores findings, while SNS delivers messages, EventBridge routes events, and Systems Manager runs the runbook.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how AWS Config and Security Hub work together to find and fix a noncompliant resource, and name one limit or tradeoff of automatic remediation.
lessons.modelAnswer: Config keeps a record of each resource's settings over time and checks them against rules, marking each resource compliant or noncompliant. Security Hub takes those results, along with findings from other tools, puts them in one format, removes duplicates and ranks them by severity against standards. Notifications come from routing rules that send high-severity events to a topic that alerts people. Remediation can be attached so a runbook fixes the setting automatically, after which Config re-evaluates to confirm the fix worked. The tradeoff is that automatic fixes can change something a live service relies on, so they should be tested and scoped, and the team should still hear when a fix runs. A rule also only catches what it was written to check, so a clean dashboard does not prove the whole account is safe.
rubricPoints: Config records configuration history and evaluates resources against rules to mark them compliant or noncompliant
Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings from several sources and ranks them by severity
Notifications are routed from events to a topic that alerts people
Automatic remediation carries risk to running services and needs scoping and testing
A rule only detects what it checks, so a clean result is not a guarantee

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a noncompliant-resource scenario across Config, Security Hub and notifications builds the pipeline understanding better than reading alone, though no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When an outside reviewer checks whether a company follows its security rules, they ask to see proof. Collecting that proof by hand, screenshot by screenshot, is slow and easy to get wrong. On AWS, two services help. One gathers proof about your own cloud accounts over time and sorts it under the rules you must meet. The other is a library where the provider publishes its own official audit reports and where you can review and accept certain legal agreements. This lesson explains what each one is for, so you know which one answers which question an auditor asks.
lessons.guessPrompt: An auditor asks, 'Show me that every database in your company was encrypted throughout last quarter.' Before reading on, where would you expect the proof to come from, and how would you show it covered the whole quarter rather than just today?
lessons.teach:
An audit is a structured check that an organization meets stated requirements. A control is one specific requirement, such as 'storage is encrypted' or 'administrator actions are logged'. A framework is a named set of controls, published by a standards body or regulator, that an auditor can test against. An assessment is a review you set up to test your environment against a framework over a chosen period. Evidence is any record showing a control was operating: a configuration record, a log, a report, or a signed agreement.

AWS Audit Manager is a service that collects evidence from your own AWS usage and organizes it. You choose a framework, create an assessment scoped to certain accounts, and the service gathers records from its data sources over the assessment period. It files that evidence under each control, so you can answer 'show me proof for this control during this window' without rebuilding the trail by hand. The key idea is that evidence accumulates over time rather than being captured once.

AWS Artifact is different. It is a self-service portal where AWS publishes its own compliance reports, including independent attestations about how AWS runs its infrastructure, and where you review and accept certain agreements that apply to your account. Artifact proves something about AWS's controls. It does not prove that your storage is encrypted.

Worked example: an auditor asks for proof that a logging control operated through March. First, create an assessment for the relevant accounts against the chosen framework. Second, confirm the relevant data sources were switched on. Third, open the logging control and review the evidence for March. Fourth, export that evidence as the audit package. Artifact is only needed if the auditor asks for the provider's own report.

Common mistake: treating an Artifact report as proof of your own configuration, or starting an assessment after the audit window and expecting March evidence to appear. Do not assume collection reaches back before the assessment existed; check what the service covers.

Consequence: evidence is only as complete as the data sources enabled while the assessment ran, so gaps found late usually cannot be filled in afterward.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's bank partner asks for proof that AWS itself runs its infrastructure under independent review, for a vendor-risk file. The team follows these steps: (1) sign in and open AWS Artifact, the self-service portal for AWS's own compliance reports; (2) find the independent report in the portal and check its date; (3) [missing step]; (4) share the report with the bank under the existing confidentiality terms. Which step correctly fills the gap?
choices: Check the report's stated scope and confirm it covers the AWS services the startup actually uses
Export the startup's CloudTrail logs and attach them, because the bank needs records of the startup's own settings
Create a new Audit Manager assessment so that the report is generated from the startup's account activity
Use the report as proof that the startup's own customer databases are encrypted, since it covers AWS's infrastructure
questions.why: Artifact reports describe AWS's own controls, so the right check is whether the report's scope actually includes the services in use before relying on it.

questions.prompt: A compliance lead at a regional insurer says: 'We turned on our Audit Manager assessment last week, and it has already gathered evidence from our own accounts.' Which statement best describes how the service collects evidence?
choices: It downloads the cloud provider's independent audit reports and stores them under your account's controls.
It captures a single snapshot of every control at the moment the assessment is created and never updates it.
It gathers records from its data sources over the assessment period and files them under each control, so evidence builds up over time.
It scans the public internet for misconfigured resources and reports only the failures.
questions.why: Audit Manager accumulates evidence from your own usage across the assessment period, filed under the matching controls, rather than capturing it once or pulling provider reports.

questions.prompt: A team creates an assessment on 10 January to cover an audit window running from the previous July through December. When they open a control on 12 January, they find almost no evidence for July to December and assume the service will fill that in later. What is the most accurate response?
choices: Recognize that evidence depends on data sources enabled while the assessment ran, so earlier gaps usually cannot be filled, and check coverage before assuming any history exists.
Delete the assessment and recreate it, which causes the service to reprocess the full prior year.
Wait a few days, since the service backfills missing history automatically once an assessment is active.
Accept an AWS Artifact agreement, which unlocks the earlier evidence for that window.
questions.why: Evidence is limited to what the enabled data sources recorded while the assessment existed, so the team should check coverage rather than expect automatic backfill, and the first option is the mistaken belief.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks a cloud security engineer for proof that the company's own object storage buckets have encryption switched on. Which source is the right place to gather that proof?
choices: The AWS Artifact portal, because it holds the provider's attestation about storage
A signed agreement accepted in Artifact, since agreements prove technical settings
The provider's public compliance report, which lists each customer's bucket settings
The company's Audit Manager assessment, which collects evidence from the company's own configuration and usage
questions.why: Audit Manager collects evidence from your own environment, whereas Artifact only proves something about the provider's controls and cannot prove your bucket settings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to audits when you would use Audit Manager instead of Artifact, and name one limit of collected evidence that they must plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Audit Manager is for proof about our own accounts. I would create an assessment against the framework the auditors use, scope it to the relevant accounts, and let it collect configuration and activity records over the audit period, filed under each control. Artifact is for proof about AWS itself: its independent compliance reports and the agreements we accept. If an auditor asks whether our storage is encrypted, the answer comes from Audit Manager evidence. If they ask for the provider's own attestation report about its infrastructure, that comes from Artifact. The limit to plan around is timing and coverage. Evidence reflects what the enabled data sources recorded while the assessment ran, so an assessment started after the audit period will not hold that period's proof. We should start early and verify coverage before the audit begins.
rubricPoints: Audit Manager collects and organizes evidence about the organization's own AWS usage against a chosen framework.
Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports and agreements, which prove things about AWS's controls rather than ours.
Evidence depends on time and data sources: an assessment only holds what was collected while it ran from enabled sources.
Uses the terms control, framework, and evidence correctly in plain words.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly service facts and the difference between two services, which reading covers best, and no listed mission or planned engine practises audit evidence collection.

lessons.plain: A review of how a cloud system is built, measured against a checklist of good practice. Instead of asking whether something works today, you ask whether it is set up to hold up under attack, mistakes and growth.
